title: Axiomatic Incompatibility Between Thermal Equilibrium and Volume-Dependent Entropy in Ideal Gas Theory
summary: A rigorous macroscopic analysis of classical thermodynamics reveals an overlooked contradiction at the foundations of ideal gas theory: the traditional volume dependent formula for entropy violates the fundamental axiom of thermal equilibrium during reversible isothermal processes. This paper resolves this inconsistency by establishing a strict operational distinction between strictly isothermal and quasi isothermal processes. We show that in order for the perfect gas to be strictly consistent with the laws of classical thermodynamics, the thermodynamic entropy of a perfect gas must be a function of temperature only. This independence of volume is also confirmed by a new analysis of the adiabatic free expansion of an ideal gas, which is found to be intrinsically reversible. To reconcile these results with standard thermodynamic practice, we introduce the concept of a pseudo isothermal process (a finite sequence of small adiabatic and isochoric steps) and show that the classical equations for work and heat apply rigorously to these real processes, as opposed to strictly isothermal ones. We conclude by discussing the profound implications of these findings for statistical mechanics, showing that while the corrected thermodynamic entropy is in perfect agreement with Maxwell's kinetic theory, it is essentially different from the Planck Boltzmann formula. Thus, thermodynamic entropy and statistical microstate counting are two different physical quantities, and the present analysis provides a simple way to free classical thermodynamics from the paradoxes of microscopic disorder.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the standard volume-dependent entropy of an ideal gas contradicts the axiom of thermal equilibrium in reversible isothermal processes, and that thermodynamic entropy of a perfect gas must depend on temperature only. This is supported by reinterpreting adiabatic free expansion as reversible, introducing "pseudo isothermal" processes to recover classical work/heat equations, and concluding that thermodynamic entropy differs fundamentally from the Planck-Boltzmann statistical formula.
AI.motivation: The authors claim a foundational contradiction in ideal gas theory: the traditional volume-dependent entropy formula violates the fundamental axiom of thermal equilibrium during reversible isothermal processes. They aim to resolve this inconsistency and free classical thermodynamics from paradoxes associated with microscopic disorder.
AI.method: A macroscopic, axiomatic analysis of classical thermodynamics. The authors draw a strict operational distinction between strictly isothermal and quasi-isothermal processes, reanalyze the adiabatic free expansion of an ideal gas, and introduce the concept of a pseudo isothermal process defined as a finite sequence of small adiabatic and isochoric steps.
AI.result: The analysis concludes that the thermodynamic entropy of a perfect gas must be a function of temperature only, independent of volume. Adiabatic free expansion is found to be intrinsically reversible. The classical work and heat equations are shown to apply rigorously to pseudo isothermal (real) processes rather than strictly isothermal ones. The corrected entropy agrees with Maxwell's kinetic theory but differs essentially from the Planck-Boltzmann formula.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamic entropy and statistical microstate counting are two distinct physical quantities. The proposed framework reconciles classical thermodynamics with kinetic theory while eliminating paradoxes of microscopic disorder, with profound implications for statistical mechanics.

title: Efficiency fluctuations in quantum heat engines with non-quasi-static adiabatic strokes
summary: We have presented an analytical and numerical study of efficiency fluctuations in quantum Carnot and Otto engines with pistons operating under non-quasi-static adiabatic expansion and compression processes at constant speed, along with quasi-static isothermal (for the Carnot engine) or isochoric processes (for the Otto engine). We have considered the two-point measurement scheme during the adiabatic strokes in this regard. By considering each of the pistons as a single quantum particle in a 1-D box with a non-quasi-statically movable boundary, we capture the stochastic nature of the work output resulting from the unitary evolution of the quantum mechanical state of the system during non-equilibrium processes. Furthermore, we have explicitly shown how the piston speed during quantum non-equilibrium strokes introduces additional quantum fluctuations that modify the average efficiency of both the engines.

AI.tldr: Analytical and numerical study of efficiency fluctuations in quantum Carnot and Otto engines with non-quasi-static adiabatic strokes, showing that piston speed introduces additional quantum fluctuations that modify average efficiency.
AI.motivation: Quantum engines are typically analyzed under quasi-static assumptions, but real engines operate with finite-speed (non-quasi-static) processes. Understanding how non-equilibrium adiabatic strokes affect efficiency fluctuations is essential for characterizing realistic quantum thermal machines.
AI.method: An analytical and numerical study of quantum Carnot and Otto engines. Non-quasi-static adiabatic expansion and compression at constant speed are combined with quasi-static isothermal (Carnot) or isochoric (Otto) processes. A two-point measurement scheme is applied during the adiabatic strokes. Each piston is modeled as a single quantum particle in a 1-D box with a non-quasi-statically movable boundary, capturing stochastic work output from unitary evolution of the quantum state during non-equilibrium processes.
AI.result: The stochastic nature of work output arising from non-equilibrium adiabatic strokes is captured via the two-point measurement scheme, and the piston speed during non-equilibrium strokes is shown explicitly to introduce additional quantum fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Piston speed in quantum non-equilibrium strokes introduces additional quantum fluctuations that modify the average efficiency of both the quantum Carnot and Otto engines.

title: A general framework for crystallization in maximal hard-core models
summary: We study general maximal hard-core models on periodic lattice-type graphs. While for standard models, phase coexistence may arise for high activity, for maximal models this behavior may occur also for sufficiently low activity values. Relying on the concept of volume allocation, we develop a {\em unified set of assumptions} that imply the Peierls condition, a convergent cluster expansion for the partition function, and hence the conclusions of Pirogov-Sinai theory for this class of models. We further check these assumptions for a number of examples including standard lattice-type periodic graphs, proving crystallization for both high and low activity. We also derive estimates for the values of activity that bound the phase coexistence regions in the phase diagram, rewriting for this purpose the proof of a technical result in the derivation of Pirogov-Sinai theory.

AI.tldr: A unified set of assumptions based on volume allocation yields the Peierls condition and a convergent cluster expansion for maximal hard-core models on periodic lattice-type graphs, extending Pirogov-Sinai theory to cover crystallization at both high and low activity, with bounds on phase-coexistence regions.
AI.motivation: Standard hard-core models exhibit phase coexistence only at high activity, whereas maximal models can show this behavior even at sufficiently low activity. Existing Pirogov-Sinai machinery was not formulated to handle this maximal-model regime uniformly, so a unifying framework was needed to treat both regimes and to estimate where phase coexistence occurs.
AI.method: The authors introduce the concept of volume allocation to formulate a unified set of assumptions. These assumptions are shown to imply the Peierls condition and a convergent cluster expansion for the partition function, which then yields the conclusions of Pirogov-Sinai theory. The assumptions are verified on a range of examples, including standard lattice-type periodic graphs. The proof of a technical result in the derivation of Pirogov-Sinai theory is rewritten to obtain estimates on the activity values bounding phase-coexistence regions.
AI.result: The unified assumptions are verified for numerous examples, including standard lattice-type periodic graphs, proving crystallization for both high and low activity. Estimates for the activity values bounding the phase-coexistence regions in the phase diagram are derived via a rewritten technical proof in the Pirogov-Sinai derivation.
AI.conclusion: Volume allocation provides a general, unified route to Peierls condition and cluster-expansion convergence for maximal hard-core models on periodic lattice-type graphs, extending Pirogov-Sinai theory to crystallization at high and low activity and giving quantitative bounds on phase-coexistence regions.

title: High-resolution mapping of the phase boundary of the honeycomb-lattice Blume--Capel ferromagnet
summary: We present a high-resolution numerical study of the spin-1 Blume--Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice ($z=3$). Wang--Landau estimates of the joint density of states $Ω(E_1,E_2)$, combined with field mixing, are used to map the first-order transition line and locate the tricritical point at $(Δ_t,T_t)=[1.4819(2),\,0.4022(7)]$. Histogram reweighting of Metropolis simulations for $L=36$ and $48$ provides an independent consistency check, with a crossing temperature near $0.4039$, compatible with the Wang--Landau extrapolation. From the field-mixing analysis we obtain $r=-1.586(19)$, while the slope of the multicanonical coexistence line yields the consistent and more precise estimate $r=-1.587(5)$. Normalizing by the zero-temperature field $Δ_0=zJ/2$, the available honeycomb, square, triangular, and simple-cubic estimates cluster near $r/Δ_0\simeq-1.06$, corresponding to a magnitude about $6\%$ larger than the mean-field value $-1$; no systematic dependence on coordination number or dimensionality is resolved over the range examined. Finite-size scaling of $σ_Q$ gives $y_t=1.795(7)$, consistent with the tricritical Ising value $9/5$, while the fourth-order cumulant scaling is compatible with $y_g=4/5$. Deep in the first-order regime, the cumulant approaches the expected two-phase limit $U_Q\to2/3$. Multicanonical simulations up to $L=64$, using weights constructed directly from the Wang--Landau density of states for $L\le24$ and rescaled and refined for larger systems, yield an interface-tension exponent $μ=1.265(26)$, consistent with the tricritical prediction $(d-1)/y_g=5/4$. Finally, we map the continuous branch of the phase boundary from the same density-of-states data, obtaining $T_c(Δ=0)=1.157$; estimates sufficiently close to the tricritical point are affected by crossover from Ising to tricritical scaling.

AI.tldr: High-resolution Wang–Landau and multicanonical study of the spin-1 Blume–Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice locates the tricritical point, measures the field-mixing (or coexistence-line slope) parameter r ≈ −1.587, and confirms tricritical Ising exponents y_t = 9/5, y_g = 4/5, and μ = 5/4.
AI.motivation: The spin-1 Blume–Capel ferromagnet exhibits a tricritical point whose universality and the field-mixing/relevant scaling-field parameters are of interest, but precise estimates—particularly the universal ratio r/Δ_0 across lattices and dimensions—remain scarce for the honeycomb lattice (z=3).
AI.method: Wang–Landau estimation of the joint density of states Ω(E_1,E_2) with field mixing to map the first-order line and locate the tricritical point; histogram reweighting of Metropolis simulations at L=36,48 as an independent check; multicanonical coexistence-line slope for r; finite-size scaling of σ_Q and the fourth-order cumulant; multicanonical simulations up to L=64 using rescaled/refined Wang–Landau weights.
AI.result: Tricritical point at (Δ_t,T_t)=[1.4819(2),0.4022(7)]; crossing temperature ≈0.4039; r = −1.586(19) from field mixing and r = −1.587(5) from the coexistence-line slope; r/Δ_0 ≈ −1.06 across honeycomb, square, triangular, and simple-cubic lattices (~6% above mean-field −1) with no resolved dependence on coordination or dimensionality; y_t = 1.795(7) ≈ 9/5; y_g ≈ 4/5; U_Q → 2/3 in the two-phase limit; interface-tension exponent μ = 1.265(26) ≈ 5/4; continuous branch gives T_c(Δ=0) = 1.157, with crossover from Ising to tricritical scaling near the tricritical point.
AI.conclusion: The honeycomb Blume–Capel tricritical behavior is fully consistent with tricritical Ising universality (y_t = 9/5, y_g = 4/5, μ = 5/4), and the normalized field-mixing parameter r/Δ_0 is approximately universal (≈ −1.06) across the studied lattices and dimensionalities.

title: Overcoming the limitations of body-ordered potentials for atomistic machine learning
summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials have become indispensable tools in atomistic simulations. The most popular models rely heavily on physical priors, such as locality, smoothness and symmetry, that are assumed to improve the accuracy and transferability of the trained models. However, recent evidence suggests that, in the data-rich regime, unconstrained models that learn symmetry from the data can achieve very competitive accuracy and computational efficiency, without sacrificing stability and generalization power. Many equivariant symmetric architectures historically rely on the assumption that the interatomic potential can be approximated well by a convergentcluster expansion, i.e., a decomposition in terms associated to atomic pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and higher-order tuples. We describe an architecture that incorporates locality, smoothness, and symmetry priors, but that -- thanks to a computationally efficient tensor product formulation -- does not assume low-order truncation of the body-ordered series.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a machine-learning interatomic potential architecture that keeps locality, smoothness, and symmetry priors but, via an efficient tensor product formulation, avoids assuming a low-order truncation of the body-ordered (cluster) expansion.
AI.motivation: Most popular machine-learning interatomic potentials embed physical priors (locality, smoothness, symmetry) to improve accuracy and transferability. Many equivariant symmetric architectures further rely on the assumption that the potential is well approximated by a convergent cluster expansion truncated at low body order. Recent evidence shows that unconstrained models learning symmetry from data can be competitive in the data-rich regime, motivating architectures that retain useful priors without restrictive low-order truncation.
AI.method: The authors describe an architecture that incorporates locality, smoothness, and symmetry priors while, thanks to a computationally efficient tensor product formulation, does not assume a low-order truncation of the body-ordered series (cluster expansion).
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture achieves prior-informed modeling without imposing the standard low-order body-order truncation, enabled by an efficient tensor product formulation.

title: Data-Driven Variable-Exponent Analysis for Photoemission Yield Spectroscopy: An Autonomous Self-Diagnosing Framework Based on Integrated Residual Metrics
comment: 30 pages, 4 figures; supplementary material (28 pages) is provided as an ancillary file. Code and sample data: https://github.com/s-yagyu/n-pys
summary: Photoemission yield spectroscopy (PYS) is widely used for evaluating the electronic states of materials. As automated materials discovery advances, unsupervised extraction of physical information from ambient-air PYS data becomes important. Conventional fixed-exponent analyses and logarithmic transformations suffer from heteroscedasticity, which destabilizes estimation in low-signal regions. To address this, we propose a data-driven analysis framework based on the 1/n-Scan method, which operates directly in the original signal space, removing the geometric bias inherent in log-transform approaches. We further integrate a self-diagnostic quality-evaluation system that quantifies estimation uncertainty with Akaike weights, together with independent residual metrics--the normalized mean absolute error (NMAE), the RMSE-to-MAE ratio (RMR), the Durbin-Watson (DW) statistic, and a macroscopic metric ($ΔR^2$)--that distinguish hardware-related data degradation from a physical-model mismatch. Applying the framework to differently doped Si and a polycrystalline Au reference in air, we demonstrate autonomous detection, without assumptions on the emission mechanism, of the breakdown of the single-component approximation in heavily doped p-type Si, arising from the overlap of two emission components with different thresholds, as a statistical anomaly--a decrease in DW below its critical value with an auxiliary increase in $ΔR^2$, despite sound NMAE and RMR--independently confirmed by a two-component fit ($Δ$AIC $\approx$ 57, DW recovering from 0.8 to 2.0). For heavily doped n-type Si, the gradual surface evolution was classified as a change within the single-component description. This framework provides a robust, self-diagnosing analysis engine for closed-loop autonomous materials exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a data-driven, self-diagnosing framework for photoemission yield spectroscopy (PYS) based on the 1/n-Scan method that analyzes signals directly in the original space, avoiding log-transform bias, and couples Akaike-weight uncertainty quantification with residual diagnostics (NMAE, RMR, DW, ΔR²) to distinguish hardware degradation from physical-model mismatch, validated on doped Si and polycrystalline Au.
AI.motivation: As automated materials discovery advances, unsupervised extraction of physical information from ambient-air PYS data becomes important. Conventional fixed-exponent analyses and logarithmic transformations suffer from heteroscedasticity, which destabilizes estimation in low-signal regions. There is a need for a robust, self-diagnosing analysis engine for closed-loop autonomous materials exploration.
AI.method: The authors propose a data-driven analysis framework based on the 1/n-Scan method, which operates directly in the original signal space, removing the geometric bias inherent in log-transform approaches. They integrate a self-diagnostic quality-evaluation system that quantifies estimation uncertainty with Akaike weights, together with independent residual metrics—the normalized mean absolute error (NMAE), the RMSE-to-MAE ratio (RMR), the Durbin-Watson (DW) statistic, and a macroscopic metric (ΔR²)—to distinguish hardware-related data degradation from physical-model mismatch.
AI.result: Applying the framework to differently doped Si and a polycrystalline Au reference in air, the authors demonstrate autonomous detection, without assumptions on the emission mechanism, of the breakdown of the single-component approximation in heavily doped p-type Si, arising from the overlap of two emission components with different thresholds, as a statistical anomaly—a decrease in DW below its critical value with an auxiliary increase in ΔR², despite sound NMAE and RMR—independently confirmed by a two-component fit (ΔAIC ≈ 57, DW recovering from 0.8 to 2.0). For heavily doped n-type Si, the gradual surface evolution was classified as a change within the single-component description.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a robust, self-diagnosing analysis engine for closed-loop autonomous materials exploration, enabling unsupervised extraction of physical information from PYS data while distinguishing hardware-related degradation from physical-model mismatch.

title: Omnisolver: An extensible interface to Ising spin-glass and QUBO solvers: adding a distributed GPU brute-force plugin
summary: This software update extends Omnisolver with \texttt{omnisolver-bruteforce}, a first-class plugin for exact exhaustive search of QUBO and Ising instances on CUDA-enabled GPUs. The update contributes three components: packaging of the single-GPU brute-force kernel of [Computer Physics Communications 260, 107728, 2021] as a first-class Omnisolver plugin with a uniform Python and CLI interface, a Ray-based distributed framework that splits the search into $2^{k}$ fixed-variable subproblems and dispatches them across multiple GPUs and hosts, with a controller that gathers and merges partial results, and numerical stabilization of the fast \texttt{float32} ground-state path through compensated incremental updates, periodic exact energy re-anchoring, and best-buffer refresh. Stabilization activates automatically for $N \geq 40$ leaving the public sampler API is unchanged. On dense random Ising instances we measure exhaustive solve times up to $N=60$ on $8\times$ NVIDIA H100 (96 GB) GPUs, reaching $\approx\!3.15$ days at $N=60$ in close agreement with the empirical $t_{N+1}=2\,t_N$ doubling rule, with the distributed sampler reaching the full $\approx\!8\times$ speedup over a single H100 from $N\!\gtrsim\!44$ onwards. The plugin thereby serves as a practical ground-truth oracle for state-of-the-art classical heuristics such as the Simulated Bifurcation Machine.

AI.tldr: The paper presents omnisolver-bruteforce, a first-class Omnisolver plugin that performs exact exhaustive search of QUBO and Ising instances on CUDA GPUs, with a Ray-based distributed framework scaling across multiple GPUs/hosts and numerical stabilization enabling exhaustive solving up to N=60.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art classical heuristics such as the Simulated Bifurcation Machine need a reliable ground-truth oracle to validate optimality, and no scalable, accessible exact solver existed for large QUBO/Ising instances across GPUs and hosts.
AI.method: The update packages a single-GPU brute-force kernel as an Omnisolver plugin with uniform Python and CLI interfaces, adds a Ray-based distributed framework that splits the search into 2^k fixed-variable subproblems across multiple GPUs/hosts with a controller merging partial results, and applies numerical stabilization of the float32 ground-state path via compensated incremental updates, periodic exact energy re-anchoring, and best-buffer refresh, auto-activated for N >= 40 without API changes.
AI.result: On dense random Ising instances, exhaustive solve times reach up to N=60 on 8x NVIDIA H100 (96 GB) GPUs, about 3.15 days at N=60, closely following the empirical t_{N+1}=2 t_N doubling rule; the distributed sampler achieves the full ~8x speedup over a single H100 from N >= 44 onwards.
AI.conclusion: omnisolver-bruteforce provides a practical GPU-accelerated, distributed exact solver that serves as a ground-truth oracle for evaluating state-of-the-art classical heuristics.

title: Time-Domain Analysis of Surface Acoustic Wave Magnetoelectric Sensors
summary: The transient response of surface acoustic wave sensors is important for understanding their dynamic behavior, propagation delay, and response to time-varying signals. In this work, the time-domain propagation characteristics of a magnetoelectric SAW sensor based on a multilayer Love-wave delay line are investigated using complementary numerical and experimental approaches. Time-domain analysis is employed to determine the delay time and to extract the phase and group velocities, while frequency-domain analysis provides an independent characterization of the wave dispersion. Both numerically and experimentally, the phase and group velocities are found to differ, reflecting the dispersion of the Love wave in the multilayer structure. At the operating frequency of 146 MHz, the simulated group velocity obtained from wave-field tracking agrees within 0.4% with the value determined from the frequency-domain dispersion relation. The simulated delay time and group velocity also show good agreement with experiment, with deviations of 2.7% in delay time and 0.9% in group velocity. These results demonstrate the consistency of the time- and frequency-domain analyses and provide a quantitative characterization of the transient propagation behavior of SAW sensors.

AI.tldr: Time- and frequency-domain analyses of a magnetoelectric Love-wave SAW delay line yield consistent phase/group velocities and delay times, validated numerically and experimentally at 146 MHz.
AI.motivation: Understanding the transient response of surface acoustic wave (SAW) sensors is necessary to characterize their dynamic behavior, propagation delay, and response to time-varying signals, yet quantitative characterization of transient propagation in multilayer Love-wave devices is limited.
AI.method: Complementary numerical and experimental study of a magnetoelectric SAW sensor based on a multilayer Love-wave delay line. Time-domain analysis determines delay time and extracts phase and group velocities via wave-field tracking; frequency-domain analysis independently characterizes wave dispersion.
AI.result: Phase and group velocities differ in both simulation and experiment, confirming Love-wave dispersion in the multilayer structure. At 146 MHz, simulated group velocity from wave-field tracking agrees within 0.4% with that from the frequency-domain dispersion relation. Simulated delay time and group velocity match experiment with deviations of 2.7% and 0.9%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Time- and frequency-domain analyses are mutually consistent, providing a quantitative characterization of the transient propagation behavior of SAW sensors.

title: Magnetic localization and spectral asymmetry of a charged particle at a screw dislocation
summary: We study a charged particle moving outside a spiral (screw) dislocation in a uniform magnetic field. Although the geometry is locally Euclidean, its global screw identification couples the conserved axial and azimuthal quantities through the combination \(\mathcal{J}=\ell-βk\) After eliminating the cyclic coordinates, the radial motion is governed by an inverse-square term determined by $\mathcal{J}$ and a harmonic confining term generated by the magnetic field. The corresponding reduced quantum problem is exactly solvable for $q\mathcal{B}_0\neq0$, yielding an equally spaced spectrum with an orientation-dependent energy shift. The radial probability density depends on $\mathcal{J}$, and opposite values of the screw-modified quantum number have identical spatial profiles but different energies for a fixed magnetic-field orientation. The radial size scales as \(\sqrt{\langle r^2\rangle_n}\propto |q\mathcal{B}_0|^{-1/2}\), with the magnetic length setting the localization scale. At $q\mathcal{B}_0=0$, the confining term vanishes, and the problem reduces to a scale-free inverse-square system. Thus, the screw parameter enters the dynamics through the global coupling of the conserved axial and azimuthal quantities, whereas the magnetic field provides radial confinement and its orientation determines the spectral asymmetry.

AI.tldr: A charged particle outside a screw dislocation in a uniform magnetic field reduces to an exactly solvable radial problem with an equally spaced spectrum, orientation-dependent energy shift, and spectral asymmetry set by the field orientation.
AI.motivation: To understand how a globally non-trivial but locally Euclidean screw dislocation geometry affects charged-particle dynamics, specifically how its global screw identification couples conserved axial and azimuthal quantities and reshapes the quantum spectrum in a magnetic field.
AI.method: Analyze a charged particle outside a spiral (screw) dislocation in a uniform magnetic field. Exploit the global screw identification that couples axial and azimuthal conserved quantities via J = ℓ − βk. Eliminate cyclic coordinates to obtain a reduced radial problem governed by an inverse-square term (from J) plus a harmonic confining term (from the magnetic field), then solve the reduced quantum problem exactly for qB₀ ≠ 0.
AI.result: For qB₀ ≠ 0 the reduced quantum problem is exactly solvable, giving an equally spaced spectrum with an orientation-dependent energy shift. The radial probability density depends on J; opposite values of the screw-modified quantum number yield identical spatial profiles but different energies at fixed field orientation. The radial size scales as √⟨r²⟩ₙ ∝ |qB₀|^(−1/2), with the magnetic length setting the localization scale. At qB₀ = 0 the confining term vanishes and the system becomes a scale-free inverse-square problem.
AI.conclusion: The screw parameter influences dynamics solely through the global coupling of conserved axial and azimuthal quantities, while the magnetic field supplies radial confinement and its orientation determines the spectral asymmetry.

title: Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks
summary: The Lyapunov spectrum of a nonlinear recurrent neural network with random asymmetric couplings is calculated in the limit $N\to\infty$. The calculation is based on a finite-$N$ identity that expresses the cumulative distribution of Lyapunov exponents as a response function of the tangent-space dynamics, with the tangent trajectory selected by a minimum-norm condition rather than by an initial condition. A cavity method then determines this response function at large $N$ through a self-consistent single-site problem. This result establishes that the chaos in this network is extensive and gives access to diffeomorphism-invariant properties of the dynamics. This work was done in collaboration with the AI models GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5.

AI.tldr: The paper computes the full Lyapunov spectrum of a random asymmetric recurrent neural network in the infinite-width limit, showing that the chaos is extensive and that the exponents admit a diffeomorphism-invariant description.
AI.motivation: Chaos in large random recurrent neural networks is typically characterized only by the maximal Lyapunov exponent; a complete, analytical description of the entire Lyapunov spectrum for asymmetric couplings had remained elusive.
AI.method: The authors start from a finite-N identity expressing the cumulative distribution of Lyapunov exponents as a response function of the tangent-space dynamics, with the tangent trajectory fixed by a minimum-norm condition instead of an initial condition. A cavity (mean-field) method then reduces the large-N response function to a self-consistent single-site problem.
AI.result: The calculation yields the Lyapunov spectrum in the limit N to infinity and demonstrates that the chaotic behavior of the network is extensive.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides access to diffeomorphism-invariant properties of the dynamics, offering a full-spectrum characterization of chaos in random asymmetric recurrent networks.

title: Supercurrent as a bulk probe for topological phase
summary: Distinguishing trivial from topological superconducting phase remains a central and contested experimental challenge, since most existing probes infer the bulk phase transition indirectly, from boundary signatures that can be sensitive to local physics. Here, we propose an alternative that probes the bulk topological phase and is based on supercurrent response. We study a one-dimensional Rashba spin-orbit-coupled superconducting nanowire with an applied magnetic field that opens a topological gap. We show that for strong spin-orbit coupling, the superfluid stiffness, and consequently the supercurrent, is suppressed by a factor of two inside the topological phase, producing a non-monotonic signature of the bulk phase transition as a function of chemical potential. We further use a low-energy helical model to understand this suppression analytically. Our results show that the bulk topological phase transition can be detected through kinetic inductance measurements.

AI.tldr: The authors propose probing the bulk topological phase transition in a Rashba spin-orbit-coupled superconducting nanowire via supercurrent response, showing a factor-of-two suppression of superfluid stiffness inside the topological phase.
AI.motivation: Existing probes infer the topological phase transition indirectly from boundary signatures sensitive to local physics, making it hard to distinguish trivial from topological superconducting phases. A bulk-sensitive probe is needed.
AI.method: Study a one-dimensional Rashba spin-orbit-coupled superconducting nanowire under an applied magnetic field that opens a topological gap. Compute the superfluid stiffness and supercurrent, and use a low-energy helical model for analytical understanding.
AI.result: For strong spin-orbit coupling, the superfluid stiffness (and hence supercurrent) is suppressed by a factor of two inside the topological phase, yielding a non-monotonic signature of the bulk phase transition as a function of chemical potential.
AI.conclusion: The bulk topological phase transition can be detected through kinetic inductance measurements.

title: Theory of Topologically Ordered Superfluids in 2+1 Dimensions
summary: Topologically ordered superfluids (TOSFs) support deconfined, gapped anyonic excitations while remaining gapless because of Goldstone modes. We develop a general framework for characterizing their topological data in $(2+1)$-dimensional bosonic systems with spontaneously broken charge ${\rm U}(1)_{\rm c}$ symmetry. Gauging ${\rm U}(1)_{\rm c}$ maps a TOSF to a gapped topological order enriched by a dual ${\rm U}(1)_{\rm dual}$ symmetry with vanishing Hall conductance, while gauging ${\rm U}(1)_{\rm dual}$ recovers the TOSF. This two-way mapping allows the topological data of the TOSF, including the condensate charge, deconfined anyon content, and topological properties of vortices, to be systematically encoded using the algebraic framework of symmetry-enriched topological orders. In particular, superfluid vortices share the topological properties of flux defects associated with the residual discrete symmetry in the gapped anyon sector. We develop complementary algebraic and field-theoretic formulations of this framework, with the latter also suggesting a natural transition to a gapped topologically ordered phase. Additionally, using parton constructions, we present examples of TOSFs with non-Abelian vortices in bosonic systems.

AI.tldr: The authors build a general framework to characterize topological data of topologically ordered superfluids (TOSFs) in (2+1)D bosonic systems with broken U(1)_c symmetry, by mapping TOSFs to gapped symmetry-enriched topological orders via a two-way gauging duality.
AI.motivation: TOSFs host deconfined gapped anyonic excitations yet remain gapless due to Goldstone modes, so their topological data (condensate charge, deconfined anyon content, vortex properties) is not captured by standard gapped topological order frameworks. A systematic characterization was lacking.
AI.method: The framework gauges U(1)_c to map a TOSF to a gapped topological order enriched by a dual U(1)_dual symmetry with vanishing Hall conductance, and gauging U(1)_dual recovers the TOSF. This two-way mapping encodes TOSF topological data in the algebraic framework of symmetry-enriched topological orders. Complementary algebraic and field-theoretic formulations are developed, and parton constructions are used to build examples.
AI.result: The condensate charge, deconfined anyon content, and topological properties of vortices are systematically encoded. Superfluid vortices are shown to share topological properties of flux defects tied to the residual discrete symmetry in the gapped anyon sector. The field-theoretic formulation suggests a natural transition to a gapped topologically ordered phase, and parton constructions yield examples of TOSFs with non-Abelian vortices in bosonic systems.
AI.conclusion: Gauging duality provides a unified algebraic and field-theoretic description of TOSFs, linking their vortices to flux defects of a residual discrete symmetry and enabling explicit construction of bosonic TOSFs with non-Abelian vortices.

title: Disorder-induced nuclear-transition doublet at nominally cubic $^{229}$Th sites
summary: The $^{229}$Th nuclear clock transition is inhomogeneously broadened even at sites of nominally cubic symmetry, where the electric-field gradient of the ideal lattice vanishes. We show that dilute static point-defect disorder produces a doublet with a zero at the quadrupole-free frequency. The doublet is symmetric in the isotropic approximation; size misfit point defects introduce a small lobe asymmetry without removing the zero. Charged and size-misfit defects share inverse-cube scaling and an approximately common normalized profile, whose width separates into a host-controlled background and a term linear in the $^{229}$Th density. In a heavily doped $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ crystal [Nature 657, 626 (2026)], the thorium-linked contribution is comparable to the measured 1.1 MHz width; in a lightly doped crystal [arXiv:2606.08870], the 0.9 MHz width bounds the host background. Neither spectrum shows the predicted dip, which points to the presence of extended defects in both crystals. If the predicted dip is resolved, it can provide a nuclear-clock discriminator referenced to the quadrupole-free nuclear transition frequency.

AI.tldr: Dilute static point-defect disorder is shown to produce a symmetric doublet (with a zero at the quadrupole-free frequency) in the inhomogeneously broadened $^{229}$Th nuclear clock transition, even at nominally cubic sites; its width splits into a host background and a thorium-density-linear term, and the absence of the predicted dip in two $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ crystals indicates extended defects.
AI.motivation: The $^{229}$Th nuclear clock transition is inhomogeneously broadened even at sites of nominally cubic symmetry, where the ideal-lattice electric-field gradient vanishes, and the microscopic origin of this broadening (and its dependence on thorium density and host) is not understood.
AI.method: Analytical modeling of dilute static point-defect disorder: point defects are treated as sources of perturbation (charged defects and size-misfit defects) acting on the $^{229}$Th quadrupole interaction, with the resulting line shape derived in the isotropic approximation and its scaling and normalized profile examined.
AI.result: Point-defect disorder yields a doublet with a zero exactly at the quadrupole-free frequency, symmetric in the isotropic approximation; size misfit introduces a small lobe asymmetry but preserves the zero. Charged and size-misfit defects share inverse-cube ($1/r^3$) scaling and a nearly common normalized profile. The doublet width decomposes into a host-controlled background plus a term linear in $^{229}$Th density. In heavily doped $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ [Nature 657, 626 (2026)] the thorium-linked term is comparable to the measured 1.1 MHz width, while in a lightly doped crystal [arXiv:2606.08870] the 0.9 MHz width bounds the host background. Neither measured spectrum shows the predicted dip, indicating extended defects in both crystals.
AI.conclusion: Point-defect disorder quantitatively accounts for the inhomogeneous broadening and its thorium-density dependence in $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$, but the missing central dip in both measured spectra points to extended defects rather than purely dilute point defects. Resolving the predicted dip would provide a nuclear-clock discriminator referenced to the quadrupole-free nuclear transition frequency.

title: Resolving the interfacial mechanical landscape of monolayer NbSe2 grown by confined epitaxy
summary: Confined epitaxy has recently emerged as a novel methodology for controlled growth of high-quality monolayer two-dimensional (2D) materials. However, mechanistic understanding remains limited to analysing nucleus adsorption and diffusion barriers. Here, I discover that van der Waals (vdW) confinement not only affects the specific adsorption and diffusion of nuclei on confined substrates but also induces strong coupling to atomic forces at the interface. Using artificial intelligence (AI) assisted density functional theory (DFT) calculations, I study how vdW confinement couples to the atomic motion of monolayer NbSe2 grown between c-plane sapphire and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN). The calculated force-electronic landscape yields large mechanical forces of +0.070 and -0.04 eV per Angstrom on Nb and Se, respectively, giving rise to a unit-cell interfacial interaction energy up to 2.4 eV, comparable to reported adsorption and diffusion energies on similar substrates. The results indicate that interfacial mechanics may explain the success of confined epitaxy. The findings suggest that tuning interfacial mechanics, and related vdW mechanochemistry, could be a promising route to high-throughput, high-quality materials synthesis.

AI.tldr: Van der Waals confinement in confined epitaxy induces strong interfacial atomic-force coupling, not just adsorption/diffusion effects; AI-assisted DFT on monolayer NbSe2 between sapphire and h-BN reveals large mechanical forces and interfacial interaction energies that may explain confined epitaxy's success.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic understanding of confined epitaxy for monolayer 2D materials has been limited to nucleus adsorption and diffusion barriers, overlooking how vdW confinement couples to atomic motion and interfacial forces.
AI.method: AI-assisted density functional theory (DFT) calculations of monolayer NbSe2 grown between c-plane sapphire and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN); computation of the force-electronic landscape and interfacial interaction energies.
AI.result: Large mechanical forces of +0.070 eV/Å on Nb and -0.04 eV/Å on Se, yielding a unit-cell interfacial interaction energy up to 2.4 eV, comparable to reported adsorption and diffusion energies on similar substrates.
AI.conclusion: Interfacial mechanics may explain the success of confined epitaxy; tuning interfacial mechanics and related vdW mechanochemistry could enable high-throughput, high-quality materials synthesis.

title: Markov length can diverge in systems whose universal physics is spatially Markovian
summary: Conditional mutual information (CMI) probes spatial non-Markovianity and plays a central role in a recently developed framework for defining mixed-state phases based on local reversibility. This framework sharply distinguishes exponentially decaying from algebraically decaying CMI, since the latter obstructs equivalence to a state with finite Markov length. Here we show that states that flow to the same renormalization-group (RG) fixed point can nevertheless exhibit qualitatively different CMI. Starting from a critical Gibbs state of a finite-range local classical Hamiltonian, whose CMI vanishes beyond the interaction range, we show that an RG-irrelevant perturbation that breaks detailed balance generically generates algebraically decaying CMI. Crucially, these power-law tails are cutoff-suppressed: although they lead to an infinite Markov length at every fixed lattice cutoff, they vanish as a positive power of the cutoff in the continuum limit. We construct solvable models that exhibit this phenomenon and predict that the Ising-symmetric critical point of Toom's cellular automata generically exhibits such behavior. We also find analogous cutoff-suppressed CMI in the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the long-range Ising paramagnet, in contrast with the genuine power-law CMI at the finite-temperature critical point in this same model that survives the continuum limit. We also derive a general result that in one spatial dimension, CMI decays faster than the inverse square of the buffer length if and only if the long-distance physics is Markovian.

AI.tldr: Renormalization-group-irrelevant perturbations that break detailed balance can generate algebraically decaying conditional mutual information (CMI) even in states flowing to the same RG fixed point, but these power-law tails are cutoff-suppressed and vanish in the continuum limit, unlike genuine power-law CMI at critical points.
AI.motivation: CMI probes spatial non-Markovianity and underpins a framework for defining mixed-state phases via local reversibility, which sharply separates exponentially from algebraically decaying CMI since the latter blocks equivalence to states with finite Markov length. The paper asks whether states flowing to the same RG fixed point can nonetheless display qualitatively different CMI, and how such differences behave under the continuum limit.
AI.method: Starting from a critical Gibbs state of a finite-range local classical Hamiltonian (whose CMI vanishes beyond the interaction range), the authors introduce an RG-irrelevant perturbation that breaks detailed balance and analyze its effect on CMI. They construct solvable models exhibiting the phenomenon and analyze Toom's cellular automata at its Ising-symmetric critical point, as well as the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the long-range Ising paramagnet, comparing with the genuine power-law CMI at that model's finite-temperature critical point. They also prove a general one-dimensional result relating CMI decay to Markovianity.
AI.result: The RG-irrelevant, detailed-balance-breaking perturbation generically generates algebraically decaying CMI. These power-law tails are cutoff-suppressed: they give infinite Markov length at every fixed lattice cutoff but vanish as a positive power of the cutoff in the continuum limit. Solvable models exhibit this behavior, and Toom's cellular automata Ising-symmetric critical point is predicted to show it generically. Analogous cutoff-suppressed CMI appears in the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the long-range Ising paramagnet, in contrast to the genuine power-law CMI at the finite-temperature critical point of the same model, which survives the continuum limit. In one spatial dimension, CMI decays faster than the inverse square of the buffer length if and only if the long-distance physics is Markovian.
AI.conclusion: States flowing to the same RG fixed point can have qualitatively different CMI, so algebraic decay alone does not imply obstruction to finite Markov length once cutoff dependence is accounted for. Cutoff-suppressed power-law CMI must be distinguished from genuine power-law CMI that survives the continuum limit, refining how local-reversibility-based mixed-state phases should be diagnosed.

title: Ab Initio Investigation of Excited States and Absorption Spectra of Small Mercury Clusters (Hg$_{2-5}$)
summary: We report a systematic \textit{ab initio} investigation of the excited states and absorption spectra of small mercury clusters (Hg$_{\mathrm{2-5}}$). Benchmarking multi-reference configuration interaction (MR-CISD) and equation-of-motion coupled-cluster (EOM-CCSD) methods shows that EOM-CCSD/aug-cc-PVTZ-PP reproduces atomic excitation energies within $\pm$500 cm$^{-1}$ of experiment, whereas MR-CISD deviates by about $\pm$1100 cm$^{-1}$. For the mercury dimer, EOM-CCSD potential energy curves yield absorption bands in excellent agreement with experimental transitions, while asymptotic excitation energies closely match atomic references. Extending this methodology, we present the first systematic \textit{ab initio} study of absorption spectra of Hg$_{\mathrm{3}}$, Hg$_{\mathrm{4}}$, Hg$_{\mathrm{5}}$, which display broad bands in the ranges of 37000-60000 cm$^{-1}$. The consistent agreement with experimental benchmarks and diagnostics confirming single-reference character validates EOM-CCSD as a robust approach for describing excited states and optical spectra of mercury clusters.

AI.tldr: Systematic ab initio study of excited states and absorption spectra of small mercury clusters (Hg2–5); EOM-CCSD/aug-cc-PVTZ-PP is validated as accurate and robust, and first systematic spectra for Hg3, Hg4, Hg5 are reported (broad bands at 37000–60000 cm−1).
AI.motivation: Accurate excited-state and optical-spectrum data for small mercury clusters are lacking, and it is unclear which electronic-structure method can reliably describe them given potential multi-reference character. A benchmarked approach is needed to describe their absorption spectra.
AI.method: Benchmark EOM-CCSD/aug-cc-PVTZ-PP against MR-CISD and experiment for atomic excitation energies; compute EOM-CCSD potential energy curves and absorption bands for Hg2; extend the methodology to systematically compute absorption spectra of Hg3, Hg4, Hg5; use diagnostics to assess single-reference character.
AI.result: EOM-CCSD reproduces atomic excitation energies within ±500 cm−1 of experiment, while MR-CISD deviates by ~±1100 cm−1. For Hg2, EOM-CCSD potential energy curves yield absorption bands in excellent agreement with experiment and atomic asymptotes. Hg3–Hg5 show broad absorption bands in the range 37000–60000 cm−1, consistent with experimental benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: EOM-CCSD/aug-cc-PVTZ-PP is a robust method for excited states and optical spectra of small mercury clusters; single-reference character is confirmed by diagnostics, and the first systematic absorption spectra of Hg3, Hg4, Hg5 are provided.

title: Generation, Accumulation, and Utilization of Data in the Automatically Controlled End-Station of a Soft X-ray Beamline
summary: AI is rapidly transforming materials exploration, yet reliable AI-assisted research depends on experimental data that retains their context, provenance, and machine-readable structure. High-throughput synchrotron measurements therefore require more than automated data acquisition: data generation, accumulation, and utilization must be connected within a continuous workflow. Here, we present a data-centric research framework that integrates the PIONEER system, the OMNES, and ML analysis. The PIONEER system automates sample handling, vacuum transfer, and scanning XAS at the BL08U soft X-ray beamline of NanoTerasu, systematically generating large volumes of spatially resolved spectral data. Measurement and analysis files are stored in the cloud-based ARIM-mdx data system, while OMNES manages metadata describing samples, preparation procedures, measurement conditions, instrument settings, data locations, and analysis histories. Tabular and JavaScript Object Notation formats are used according to the metadata structure, with numerical values stored separately from units to facilitate machine processing. OMNES organizes these records based on causal relationships among experimental and analytical processes, linking samples, measurements, raw data, processed data, and analysis results through a relational data model and visualizing their relationships as a graph. This causality-based organization preserves experimental and analytical provenance and clarifies how each result was derived from the preceding processes and data. The accumulated spectra can subsequently be processed using ML methods, including dimensionality reduction and materials classification, and the resulting data can be registered back into OMNES. Previously reported ML analysis of BN XAS spectra is presented as an example of the analytical workflow that can be applied to data acquired at the beamline.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a data-centric framework integrating the PIONEER automation system, the OMNES metadata/relational data system, and ML analysis to enable a continuous, provenance-preserving workflow for high-throughput synchrotron XAS at the NanoTerasu BL08U beamline.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted materials research requires experimental data that retains context, provenance, and machine-readable structure. High-throughput synchrotron measurements need more than automated acquisition: data generation, accumulation, and utilization must be connected in a single continuous workflow.
AI.method: Integration of the PIONEER system (automated sample handling, vacuum transfer, scanning XAS at the BL08U soft X-ray beamline of NanoTerasu), the OMNES and cloud-based ARIM-mdx data system for metadata management, and ML analysis. Metadata is stored in tabular and JSON formats with numerical values separated from units; OMNES uses a relational data model organized by causal relationships among experimental/analytical processes and visualizes them as a graph.
AI.result: Large volumes of spatially resolved spectral data are systematically generated; measurement and analysis files are stored in ARIM-mdx, while OMNES manages metadata on samples, preparation, measurement conditions, instrument settings, data locations, and analysis histories. Causality-based organization preserves provenance and clarifies how each result derives from prior processes and data. Accumulated spectra can be processed by ML (dimensionality reduction, materials classification), with results optionally registered back into OMNES; BN XAS spectra analysis from prior work serves as an example workflow.
AI.conclusion: The integrated framework closes the loop between automated data generation, structured metadata accumulation, and ML-based utilization, preserving experimental and analytical provenance and enabling reusable, machine-processable data for AI-assisted materials exploration.

title: Fast Angular Sweep Monostatic Radar Cross Section Computation via Model Order Reduction
summary:
The radar cross section (RCS) is a fundamental parameter in radar engineering, as it determines the detectability of a given target by a radar system. Increasing interest in very low observability (VLO) targets has arisen recently. As a result, especial effort is put in developing numerical tools to accurately predict the electromagnetic scattering from perfect electric conductor objects. Integral equation methods are commonly used in this task. However, full-wave computation of the monostatic RCS at a single angle can be rather time-consuming, nevermind computing the RCS in a specific angular interval with a fine sampling. In fact, this is what is needed in industrial applications.
  A reduced-order model for fast full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation is proposed to easily achieve fine details in the desired angular domain. An open source integral equation solver, taken into account as a black box, is used to get the electromagnetic scattering in non-penetrable objects at some specific incident angles. Several radar targets will show the possibilities and capabilities of these model order reduction approaches.

AI.tldr: A reduced-order model is proposed to accelerate full-wave monostatic RCS computation over finely sampled angular intervals using a black-box integral equation solver, demonstrated on several radar targets.
AI.motivation: RCS determines target detectability, and interest in very low observability (VLO) targets has grown. Accurate numerical prediction of electromagnetic scattering from perfect electric conductor objects is needed. Integral equation methods are standard, but full-wave computation of monostatic RCS at even a single angle is time-consuming, and computing RCS over an angular interval with fine sampling—required in industrial applications—is far more expensive.
AI.method: A reduced-order model is constructed for fast full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation. An open-source integral equation solver is treated as a black box to compute electromagnetic scattering from non-penetrable objects at selected incident angles, and model order reduction approaches are applied to capture the angular dependence with fine detail.
AI.result: Several radar targets are used to demonstrate the possibilities and capabilities of the model order reduction approaches for efficiently resolving fine angular detail in the monostatic RCS.
AI.conclusion: Reduced-order modeling enables fast, accurate full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation over desired angular domains, addressing the cost bottleneck of fine angular sampling in industrial RCS prediction.

title: Millisecond phonon lifetimes in piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators
summary: Piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators operating at gigahertz frequencies are a promising platform for quantum information processing and precision sensing, but phonon lifetimes have been limited to the microsecond range, widely attributed to the higher intrinsic loss of piezoelectric materials. Here we show that this limitation is not fundamental. Using a fabrication process informed by recent studies of defect-mediated loss in lithium niobate, we combine chemical restoration of ion-milled surfaces with a shadow-mask metallization process to produce lithium niobate phononic crystal resonators with inferred internal phonon lifetimes of up to 21 milliseconds at 3.6 gigahertz, corresponding to quality factors exceeding $4\times10^8$ ($f\cdot Q_i > 10^{18}$) at millikelvin temperatures. By systematically varying the electrode-to-resonator spacing, we demonstrate that the measured lifetime is set by external coupling between the device and the measurement circuit rather than material loss. This establishes that lithium niobate, once fabrication-induced surface damage is removed, achieves an intrinsic quality comparable to the best mechanical materials while remaining an intrinsically piezoelectric platform with strong electromechanical coupling.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that lithium niobate phononic crystal resonators can achieve internal phonon lifetimes up to 21 ms (Q > 4×10^8, f·Qi > 10^18) at 3.6 GHz and millikelvin temperatures, showing that the prior microsecond lifetime limit was due to fabrication-induced surface damage and external circuit coupling rather than fundamental material loss.
AI.motivation: Gigahertz piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators are promising for quantum information processing and precision sensing, but phonon lifetimes were limited to the microsecond range, widely believed to stem from the higher intrinsic loss of piezoelectric materials. This work challenges that assumption by testing whether the limitation is fundamental.
AI.method: Using a fabrication process informed by recent studies of defect-mediated loss in lithium niobate, the authors combined chemical restoration of ion-milled surfaces with a shadow-mask metallization process to fabricate lithium niobate phononic crystal resonators. They then systematically varied the electrode-to-resonator spacing to identify the dominant loss mechanism.
AI.result: The resonators exhibited inferred internal phonon lifetimes up to 21 ms at 3.6 GHz, corresponding to quality factors exceeding 4×10^8 (f·Qi > 10^18) at millikelvin temperatures. Varying the electrode-to-resonator spacing showed that the measured lifetime is set by external coupling between the device and the measurement circuit rather than by material loss.
AI.conclusion: Once fabrication-induced surface damage is removed, lithium niobate achieves an intrinsic quality comparable to the best mechanical materials while remaining an intrinsically piezoelectric platform with strong electromechanical coupling, indicating that low phonon lifetimes in piezoelectric resonators are not fundamental.

title: Short-Range Vector Spin Glasses: Parisi Hierarchies and Real-Space Ultrametricity
summary:
Replica symmetry breaking (RSB) is the organizing principle of mean-field spin-glass theory, yet whether a continuous Parisi hierarchy can arise in a genuinely short-range system in finite spatial dimension remains unresolved. Here we introduce a disordered model of $N$-component vector spins on a $D$-dimensional hypercubic lattice, with random matrix couplings on nearest-neighbor links and random tensor couplings on elementary plaquettes. In the large-$N$ limit, the model supports thermodynamically stable one-step, full, and one-full RSB phases, alongside replica-symmetric paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. We find that spatial locality constrains these ordered phases through two distinct infrared mechanisms. ($i$) Quenched random anisotropy destroys uniform ferromagnetism for $D\leq4$ through an Imry-Ma mechanism. ($ii$) A continuous Parisi hierarchy gives rise to replica Goldstone modes whose gaplessness is protected by a Ward identity. At leading order in $1/N$, these modes behave as a band of free spin waves, producing infrared-divergent fluctuations in $D\leq2$ and a Mermin-Wagner instability of the continuously broken phase.
  Remarkably, the Parisi hierarchy also acquires a direct real-space interpretation. For two pure states with mutual overlap $q$, a characteristic length $ξ(q)$ describes how far the differences between their frozen magnetization patterns remain correlated. Throughout a continuous sector of the Parisi hierarchy, $ξ(q)$ is independent of temperature and decreases monotonically with $q$. The ultrametric organization of pure states is therefore accompanied by an ultrametric hierarchy of real-space correlation lengths: states that separate near the root of the Parisi tree differ through long-wavelength frozen patterns, whereas states that separate farther from the root differ only on progressively shorter scales.

AI.tldr: A short-range, finite-dimensional disordered vector-spin model with random matrix and tensor couplings is shown to host thermodynamically stable replica-symmetry-breaking phases whose continuous Parisi hierarchy induces replica Goldstone modes and admits a real-space, ultrametric interpretation via overlap-dependent correlation lengths.
AI.motivation: Whether a continuous Parisi hierarchy (replica symmetry breaking, RSB) can arise in a genuinely short-range system in finite spatial dimension remains unresolved.
AI.method: Introduces an N-component vector-spin disordered model on a D-dimensional hypercubic lattice with random matrix couplings on nearest-neighbor links and random tensor couplings on elementary plaquettes; analyzes the large-N limit, infrared behavior, Ward identities, and 1/N corrections.
AI.result: Supports thermodynamically stable one-step, full, and one-full RSB phases plus replica-symmetric paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. Spatial locality constrains order via two infrared mechanisms: (i) quenched random anisotropy destroys uniform ferromagnetism for D<=4 through an Imry-Ma mechanism; (ii) a continuous Parisi hierarchy yields replica Goldstone modes whose gaplessness is protected by a Ward identity, behaving at leading 1/N order as a band of free spin waves with infrared-divergent fluctuations in D<=2 and a Mermin-Wagner instability. The hierarchy also has a real-space interpretation: for two pure states with overlap q, a characteristic length xi(q) measures correlation of frozen magnetization differences; throughout a continuous sector xi(q) is temperature-independent and monotonically decreasing with q.
AI.conclusion: The ultrametric organization of pure states is accompanied by an ultrametric hierarchy of real-space correlation lengths: states separating near the Parisi-tree root differ through long-wavelength frozen patterns, while those separating farther from the root differ on progressively shorter scales.

title: Amplitude mode in Eliashberg superconductors
summary: In the BCS theory of superconductivity the amplitude (Higgs) mode is degenerate with the pair-breaking threshold: its frequency coincides with $2Δ$, so it is an edge singularity rather than a true collective mode. This is why after a sudden weak perturbation at $t=0$ its oscillations decay algebraically as $1/\sqrt{t}$. We show that the retardation effects due to the phonon dynamics in the strong-coupling theory lift this degeneracy. The Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge $2Δ_g$, set by the spectral gap, and becomes a sharp subgap excitation. We determine its frequency from the longitudinal pair susceptibility evaluated directly on the real frequency axis, using the Eilenberger equations for Migdal--Eliashberg theory with the Einstein phonon spectrum. The response of the mass renormalization supplies at least two fifths of the displacement, and possibly all of it: with it switched off, the binding falls below the resolution of the calculation. Its consequences, however, are significant because a percent-level shift transfers about a quarter of the spectral weight of the amplitude channel out of the two-quasiparticle continuum into a discrete energy level. What experiment sees is therefore not the displacement itself but its consequence: amplitude oscillations that persist instead of decaying as $1/\sqrt{t}$.

AI.tldr: In strong-coupling superconductors, phonon retardation lifts the degeneracy between the Higgs (amplitude) mode and the pair-breaking threshold, converting the Higgs mode from an edge singularity that decays as $1/\sqrt{t}$ into a genuine sharp subgap collective mode whose oscillations persist.
AI.motivation: In BCS theory the Higgs mode is degenerate with $2\Delta$, making it an edge singularity rather than a true collective mode; this degeneracy is why its oscillations after a sudden perturbation decay algebraically as $1/\sqrt{t}$. The paper asks whether retardation from phonon dynamics in strong-coupling theory removes this degeneracy and produces a genuine, long-lived collective mode.
AI.method: The longitudinal pair susceptibility is evaluated directly on the real frequency axis using the Eilenberger equations within Migdal–Eliashberg theory with an Einstein phonon spectrum. The role of the mass-renormalization response in displacing the Higgs mode below the spectral gap $2\Delta_g$ is quantified by switching it off.
AI.result: Retardation lifts the degeneracy: the Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge $2\Delta_g$ and becomes a sharp subgap excitation. The mass-renormalization response contributes at least two fifths of the displacement (possibly all of it, since without it the binding falls below the calculation's resolution). Even a percent-level shift transfers roughly a quarter of the amplitude-channel spectral weight from the two-quasiparticle continuum into a discrete level.
AI.conclusion: The experimentally observable signature is not the displacement itself but its consequence: amplitude oscillations that persist rather than decaying as $1/\sqrt{t}$. Phonon-induced retardation thus turns the Higgs mode into a true collective mode in strong-coupling superconductors.

title: SC$^\sharp$: superconductivity intertwined with topological order
summary: Superconductivity and intrinsic topological order can intertwine in ways that go beyond simple coexistence. Here we develop a classification framework for (2+1)D gapped superconductors with condensate charge $2ne$. By focusing on the topological properties of superconducting vortices, we precisely characterize this interplay. We obtain a classification with increasing levels of intertwinement, from the well known invertible superconductors without topological order, to untwisted and twisted SC$^\ast$, and finally to SC$^{\sharp}$. Our main finding is the family SC$^{\sharp}$, in which the elementary vortex carrying $h/(2ne)$ flux cannot be factorized into an invertible superconductor vortex dressed by bulk anyons, and every elementary vortex is necessarily non-Abelian. For such phases, we also obtain no-go results: the elementary vortex sector has quantum dimension at least $\sqrt{6}$ and cannot satisfy Fibonacci fusion rules. We develop a systematic algebraic framework to obtain all these superconducting phases through anyon condensation, allowing us to construct several infinite families of examples and make connections to anyon superconductivity. Finally, we introduce primitive SC$^\sharp$ phases for which factorization of every nontrivial vortex sector is obstructed, and argue that they cannot arise by disordering the relative phases of lower-charge superconducting condensates. Our classification scheme based on vortex properties allows us to uncover new distinctions between topologically ordered superconductors and constrain how they can be realized.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a classification framework for (2+1)D gapped superconductors with condensate charge 2ne by analyzing the topological properties of their vortices, revealing a hierarchy of increasing superconductivity-topological-order intertwinement culminating in the new family SC#.
AI.motivation: Superconductivity and intrinsic topological order can intertwine in ways beyond simple coexistence, yet a systematic characterization of this interplay—especially how vortex topology encodes it—was lacking.
AI.method: Classify (2+1)D gapped superconductors with condensate charge 2ne by focusing on topological properties of superconducting vortices, organized into a hierarchy: invertible superconductors, untwisted and twisted SC*, and SC#. Develop a systematic algebraic framework via anyon condensation to obtain these phases, construct infinite families of examples, and introduce primitive SC# phases.
AI.result: The family SC# is the main finding: the elementary vortex carrying h/(2ne) flux cannot be factorized into an invertible superconductor vortex dressed by bulk anyons, and every elementary vortex is necessarily non-Abelian. No-go results: the elementary vortex sector has quantum dimension at least sqrt(6) and cannot satisfy Fibonacci fusion rules. Primitive SC# phases are identified where factorization of every nontrivial vortex sector is obstructed.
AI.conclusion: The vortex-based classification scheme uncovers new distinctions between topologically ordered superconductors and constrains how they can be realized. Primitive SC# phases cannot arise by disordering the relative phases of lower-charge superconducting condensates, linking the framework to anyon superconductivity and extending beyond simple coexistence.

title: Response of the near-threshold resonances of the $\bm{dtμ}$ molecular ion to an effective atomic $2s$--$2p$ splitting
summary: For the nonrelativistic three-body Coulomb Hamiltonian, near-threshold resonances of the deuterium--tritium muonic molecular ion ($dtμ$) are supported by the long-range dipole coupling between degenerate atomic $2s$ and $2p$ states. We study the effect of atomic $2s$--$2p$ splitting on their positions and decay widths. Three-body complex-absorbing-potential calculations resolve additional members of the $L^π=0^+$ and $1^-$ series. Their geometric spacing agrees with that expected from the $1/R^2$ dipole attraction, where $R$ is the atom--nucleus separation. To assess the effect of splitting, we scan a prescribed $2s$--$2p$ interval using an effective potential in a spin-independent, nonrelativistic Hamiltonian. This models the atomic splitting without an explicit Lamb-shift calculation. Within this model, the studied resonances lie closer to the $dμ(2s)+t$ threshold and have smaller Coulomb decay widths than in the degenerate case. At an effective interval of $0.2\eV$, the seventh $1^-$ member lies within $2\meV$ of this threshold with a full width of about $4\meV$, compared with $48$ and $15.6\meV$ at degeneracy. These values characterize the response within the tested numerical representations. Its width decreases, but its separation from the threshold decreases more strongly. The long-range analysis attributes these shifts and width reductions to modified dipole mixing. It further suggests that atomic $2s$--$2p$ splitting may truncate the infinite accumulation of resonances predicted for degenerate atomic $2s$ and $2p$ levels.

AI.tldr: Atomic 2s–2p splitting shifts dtμ near-threshold resonances closer to the dμ(2s)+t threshold and reduces their Coulomb decay widths relative to the degenerate case, and may truncate the predicted infinite resonance accumulation.
AI.motivation: Near-threshold resonances of the dtμ muonic molecular ion are supported by long-range dipole coupling between degenerate atomic 2s and 2p states. The effect of atomic 2s–2p splitting on resonance positions and decay widths was unexamined.
AI.method: Three-body complex-absorbing-potential (CAP) calculations for the nonrelativistic three-body Coulomb Hamiltonian resolve additional Lπ=0+ and 1− series members. An effective potential in a spin-independent, nonrelativistic Hamiltonian scans a prescribed 2s–2p interval, modeling the atomic splitting without explicit Lamb-shift calculation. A long-range analysis interprets dipole mixing effects.
AI.result: Resonance geometric spacing agrees with that expected from 1/R² dipole attraction, where R is the atom–nucleus separation. With splitting, resonances lie closer to the dμ(2s)+t threshold with smaller Coulomb widths than in the degenerate case. At an effective interval of 0.2 eV, the seventh 1− member lies within 2 meV of threshold with full width ~4 meV, versus 48 and 15.6 meV at degeneracy.
AI.conclusion: Atomic 2s–2p splitting shifts resonances toward threshold and reduces their widths; width decreases but threshold separation decreases more strongly. Long-range analysis attributes this to modified dipole mixing, suggesting the splitting may truncate the infinite accumulation of resonances predicted for degenerate 2s and 2p levels.

title: Hierarchical Relaxation in Large-twist-angle Moire Drives Supermoire Formation
summary: Supermoire lattices in large-angle twisted bilayers have recently been shown to emerge from periodic arrangements of commensurate stacking motifs, yet the microscopic structural mechanism governing their formation has remained unresolved. Here, we uncover the microscopic origin of supermoire order as a hierarchical lattice relaxation process. Combining force-field simulations with experimental validation via super-resolution, layer-resolved multislice electron ptychography, our results identify interlayer Se-Se repulsion at the picometer scale as the driving force, giving rise to coupled short-range (about 1 nm) moire relaxation and coexisting long-range (about 10 nm) supermoire modulation. These findings demonstrate that even picometer-scale lattice relaxation remains critical in large-angle moire systems and must be explicitly considered in understanding their emergent electronic and quantum phenomena.

AI.tldr: This work reveals the microscopic origin of supermoire order in large-angle twisted bilayers as a hierarchical lattice relaxation process driven by picometer-scale interlayer Se-Se repulsion, producing coupled 1 nm moire relaxation and 10 nm supermoire modulation.
AI.motivation: Supermoire lattices emerge from periodic arrangements of commensurate stacking motifs in large-angle twisted bilayers, but the microscopic structural mechanism governing their formation has remained unresolved. Understanding this mechanism is important because picometer-scale lattice relaxation may critically affect emergent electronic and quantum phenomena in these systems.
AI.method: The authors combine force-field simulations with experimental validation using super-resolution, layer-resolved multislice electron ptychography to investigate the structural mechanism of supermoire order formation.
AI.result: The results identify interlayer Se-Se repulsion at the picometer scale as the driving force behind supermoire order, giving rise to coupled short-range (about 1 nm) moire relaxation and coexisting long-range (about 10 nm) supermoire modulation.
AI.conclusion: Picometer-scale lattice relaxation remains critical even in large-angle moire systems and must be explicitly considered when interpreting their emergent electronic and quantum phenomena.

title: Quantum annealing of the random transverse-field Ising model in one, two, and three dimensions
summary: Quantum annealing must be sufficiently slow to prevent defect formation. We study this problem in the random transverse-field Ising model via the adiabatic theorem to obtain the limiting rate at which defect formation can be avoided. Our approach based on the strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG) technique views the annealing process as a gradual aggregation of strongly coupled clusters, giving access to the elementary events of error formation. We present a scaling theory of the statistics of these events in general dimensions and confront it to an extensive numerical analysis carried out in one, two, and three dimensions by an efficient implementation of the SDRG method. This approach is also validated by exact diagonalization in one dimension by means of the free-fermion technique. Our results consistently show a logarithmically slow decrease of the error density with the annealing time, characterized by the dimension-dependent critical exponents of the corresponding infinite-disorder fixed point of the model. Furthermore, we provide a map of individual events of potential defect formation in the excitation energy - control parameter plane, which may help in the design of optimal annealing paths.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the adiabatic theorem and the strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG) to determine the limiting quantum annealing rate that avoids defect formation in the random transverse-field Ising model, deriving a scaling theory of defect-formation events and validating it numerically in 1D, 2D, and 3D.
AI.motivation: Quantum annealing must proceed slowly enough to prevent defect (error) formation, so it is important to identify the limiting annealing rate and understand the elementary events that generate defects.
AI.method: The authors combine the adiabatic theorem with the SDRG technique, viewing annealing as gradual aggregation of strongly coupled clusters and identifying elementary error-formation events. They develop a scaling theory of the statistics of these events in general dimensions and test it with extensive numerical SDRG simulations in one, two, and three dimensions, cross-validated by exact diagonalization via the free-fermion technique in one dimension.
AI.result: The error density decreases logarithmically slowly with annealing time, governed by dimension-dependent critical exponents of the infinite-disorder fixed point of the model. A map of individual potential defect-formation events in the excitation-energy–control-parameter plane is also provided.
AI.conclusion: Defect formation in the random transverse-field Ising model is controlled by infinite-disorder criticality, yielding logarithmically slow error reduction with annealing time; the event map may aid the design of optimal annealing paths.

title: Visualizing Three-Dimensional Quantum Fluctuations of Ground-State C$_3$H$_4$ via Deep Sub-Angstrom Coulomb Explosion Imaging
summary: Coulomb explosion imaging (CEI) is a powerful tool for determining static geometries of isolated gas-phase molecules. In this work, taking allene and propyne as prototype, we demonstrate sub-angstrom resolution achieved with highly charged ion-induced CEI. Using 41.9 keV/u Xe$^{20+}$ beam, minute variations of CC single, double and triple bond lengths are clearly visualized, indicating that an ultrahigh resolution of 0.1 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ is achieved. This unprecedented resolution not only makes it possible to distinguish CC bonds with different bond orders, but also lays a solid foundation for direct observation of quantum fluctuations inherent to 3D structure of a ground-state molecule. Notably, the coupled collective motion of the two CH$_2$ moieties spaced by a central carbon within allene is unambiguously visualized in our measurements.

AI.tldr: Highly charged ion-induced Coulomb explosion imaging of allene and propyne achieves ~0.1 Å resolution, resolving CC bond-length differences by bond order and visualizing coupled CH2 collective motion.
AI.motivation: Coulomb explosion imaging (CEI) is a powerful tool for determining static geometries of isolated gas-phase molecules.
