The motivation is to push CEI resolution high enough to distinguish minute bond-length differences, resolve different bond orders, and enable direct observation of quantum fluctuations and correlated motion in ground-state molecules.
AI.method: Using allene and propyne as prototypes, the authors applied highly charged ion-induced Coulomb explosion imaging with a 41.9 keV/u Xe20+ beam to trigger multiple ionization and subsequent fragmentation, and measured the fragment-ion momenta to reconstruct molecular geometry.
AI.result: Minute variations of CC single, double, and triple bond lengths were clearly visualized, indicating an ultrahigh resolution of 0.1 Å. CC bonds of different bond orders were distinguishable; the coupled collective motion of the two CH2 moieties separated by the central carbon in allene was unambiguously visualized.
AI.conclusion: Highly charged ion-induced CEI reaches sub-angstrom (0.1 Å) resolution, enabling distinction of CC bonds with different bond orders, providing a foundation for directly observing quantum fluctuations in the 3D structure of a ground-state molecule, and enabling visualization of correlated collective motion.

title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations
summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "ghost tasking," a systematic procedure that uses auxiliary tasks to make any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling parametrized Gaussian Processes with few tasks and latent functions, especially effective in inverse problems with limited data.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed machine learning, particularly parametrized Gaussian processes, is valuable in data-limited regimes. However, existing approaches are limited: they require parametrizable (controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. This work aims to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: The authors introduce "ghost tasking," using auxiliary tasks to circumvent existing limitations. They prove that ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, allowing algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required output tasks and latent functions low. They also provide syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients.
AI.result: Ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. The method is demonstrated in three experiments, with systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. Theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
AI.conclusion: Ghost tasking offers a general and effective solution for constructing parametrized Gaussian Processes in non-parametrizable systems with limited data, broadening the applicability of physics-informed machine learning.

title: High Efficiency in Large Supercurrent Rectification with Superconducting Coil
summary: Superconducting diodes (SDs) are devices that rectify supercurrent through the difference in the superconducting critical current (Ic) between forward and reverse current directions. For bringing such SDs closer to practical superconducting power electronics applications, a combination of both high rectification efficiency (η) and a large Ic difference (ΔIc) is required. Here, we propose and demonstrate a coil-shaped superconducting wire device concept to induce a large SD effect, arising from the compensation between an external magnetic field (Hext) and the field generated by the coil itself. From transport Ic measurements on coil-shaped SDs based on a Sn10-Pb90 solder wire, we achieved a η of 79% with a ΔIc of 140 A at Hext = 500 Oe (coil #2) and a η of 84% with a ΔIc of 125 A at Hext = 530 Oe (coil #3), confirming high rectification values at large supercurrents. The large-current high-efficiency SDE in the coil-shaped SDs will be highly useful for developing the potential field of supercurrent power electronics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a coil-shaped superconducting wire device that generates a large superconducting diode effect via compensation between an external magnetic field and the self-field of the coil, achieving high rectification efficiency (79–84%) at large supercurrents (ΔIc up to 140 A) in Sn10-Pb90 solder-wire devices.
AI.motivation: Practical superconducting power electronics require superconducting diodes (SDs) that simultaneously deliver high rectification efficiency (η) and a large difference in critical current (ΔIc) between forward and reverse directions. Existing approaches generally do not achieve both high η and large ΔIc at large supercurrents, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: The authors propose and demonstrate a coil-shaped superconducting wire device concept in which the superconducting diode effect arises from compensation between an applied external magnetic field (Hext) and the magnetic field generated by the coil itself. Transport critical current (Ic) measurements were performed on coil-shaped SDs fabricated from Sn10-Pb90 solder wire, with η and ΔIc evaluated as functions of Hext.
AI.result: For coil #2, a η of 79% with ΔIc of 140 A was obtained at Hext = 500 Oe; for coil #3, a η of 84% with ΔIc of 125 A was achieved at Hext = 530 Oe. These results confirm high rectification efficiency at large supercurrents in the coil-shaped devices.
AI.conclusion: The coil-shaped superconducting wire design enables a large-current, high-efficiency superconducting diode effect, making it a promising building block for the emerging field of supercurrent power electronics.

title: Hydrodynamic Anomalous Hall Effect in a Two-Dimensional Dirac Fluid
summary: In ultraclean conductors, electron-electron collisions can make transport hydrodynamic. In a Berry-curved band, these collisions can also produce two-particle coordinate shifts, which contribute to the anomalous Hall current in the presence of a transport electric field. We develop a kinetic theory of this contribution for a two-dimensional massive Dirac Fermi liquid with weak contact interactions and weak short-range disorder. The computed response is independent of interaction strength at leading Born order. Its contribution to the anomalous Hall conductivity is comparable to the thermal correction to the intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity. The existence of the momentum zero mode of the electron-electron collision integral leads to a nontrivial frequency dependence of the anomalous Hall response considered in this work. In particular, the limits of vanishing frequency (dc) and vanishing disorder do not commute. In the dc limit, the momentum response to the transport field grows inversely with the momentum relaxation rate. This allows arbitrarily weak, energy-dependent impurity scattering to produce a finite correction by coupling conserved momentum to the modes relaxed by electron-electron scattering. This correction disappears when the clean limit is taken before the zero-frequency limit. As a result, the interaction-induced Hall response retains information about the mechanism of momentum relaxation even as the overall disorder strength tends to zero.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a kinetic theory of the interaction-induced (two-particle-coordinate-shift) anomalous Hall current in a 2D massive Dirac Fermi liquid, showing that its Hall correction is comparable to the thermal correction to intrinsic AHE, and that dc and clean limits do not commute.
AI.motivation: In ultraclean conductors electron-electron collisions make transport hydrodynamic, and in a Berry-curved band these collisions generate two-particle coordinate shifts that contribute to the anomalous Hall current under a transport electric field. This contribution had not been systematically characterized, motivating a kinetic theory for a tractable model.
AI.method: Kinetic theory of a two-dimensional massive Dirac Fermi liquid with weak contact interactions and weak short-range disorder. The anomalous Hall response from electron-electron-collision-induced two-particle coordinate shifts is computed at leading Born order in the interaction and disorder, including its frequency dependence and the role of the momentum zero mode of the collision integral.
AI.result: The computed response is independent of interaction strength at leading Born order. Its contribution to the anomalous Hall conductivity is comparable to the thermal correction to the intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity. Because of the momentum zero mode of the collision integral, the dc (vanishing frequency) and clean (vanishing disorder) limits do not commute.
AI.conclusion: In the dc limit the momentum response grows inversely with the momentum relaxation rate, so arbitrarily weak energy-dependent impurity scattering yields a finite correction by coupling conserved momentum to modes relaxed by electron-electron scattering; this correction vanishes if the clean limit precedes the zero-frequency limit. Hence the interaction-induced Hall response retains information about the momentum-relaxation mechanism even as disorder strength tends to zero.

title: Spin Chain with Continuous Exponential Symmetry: Topological Phase and Beyond
summary: We study symmetric gapped ground states of one-dimensional spin $S$ chains with a continuous exponential symmetry $U(1)\rtimes\mathbb Z_2$ with integer base $q$, where the U(1) charge has a modulated unit of charge $q^{L-j}$ decaying exponentially with site $j$. The simplest model is a quantum breakdown model that can be viewed as a $q$-deformation of the XXZ Haldane spin chain. We show that the topology of their symmetric ground states crucially depends on $S$ and $q$. For integer $S$, odd $q$ allows a nontrivial $\mathbb Z_2$ Haldane-type symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase with protected edge modes, while even $q$ allows no nontrivial SPT phase. For half-odd integer $S$, odd $q$ prohibits any unique symmetric gapped ground state due to a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis obstruction, whereas even $q$ enforces a novel symmetric gapped phase which we name as the ``half-SPT" phase. Unconventionally, the half-SPT phase only has a symmetry protected edge mode on one edge, and has half of the string orders of an SPT phase. Our results uncover a new type of symmetry-protected gapped phases beyond existing classification schemes.

AI.tldr: The paper studies symmetric gapped ground states of 1D spin-S chains with a continuous exponential symmetry U(1)⋊Z2 of integer base q, realized in a quantum breakdown model (a q-deformation of the XXZ Haldane chain), showing that the ground-state topology depends jointly on S and q and revealing a novel "half-SPT" phase.
AI.motivation: Existing symmetry-protected topological (SPT) classification schemes assume ordinary (non-modulated) symmetries. The paper is motivated by the question of how modulation of the U(1) charge—here an exponentially decaying unit of charge q^{L-j}—changes the topology of symmetric gapped ground states, and whether new gapped phases beyond standard classification can arise.
AI.method: The authors analyze symmetric gapped ground states of one-dimensional spin-S chains whose symmetry is a continuous exponential U(1)⋊Z2 with integer base q and exponentially modulated charge q^{L-j}. They focus on the simplest realization, a quantum breakdown model interpretable as a q-deformation of the XXZ Haldane spin chain, and examine how the topology of the symmetric ground states depends on the spin S and the base q, using Lieb-Schultz-Mattis-type obstructions and edge-mode/string-order diagnostics.
AI.result: The topology of symmetric ground states depends crucially on S and q. For integer S: odd q supports a nontrivial Z2 Haldane-type SPT phase with protected edge modes, while even q allows no nontrivial SPT phase. For half-odd-integer S: odd q forbids any unique symmetric gapped ground state due to a Lieb-Schultz-Mattis obstruction, whereas even q enforces a novel symmetric gapped phase termed the "half-SPT" phase. The half-SPT phase unconventionally hosts a symmetry-protected edge mode on only one edge and exhibits half of the string orders of a standard SPT phase.
AI.conclusion: Modulated (exponential) continuous symmetries yield a richer landscape of symmetric gapped phases than conventional SPT classification schemes predict, including the newly identified half-SPT phase with single-edge protected modes and halved string order. The results uncover a new type of symmetry-protected gapped phase beyond existing classification schemes.

title: Local polarization control of optical tweezer arrays
summary: Optical tweezer arrays trapping ultracold atoms and molecules are a versatile quantum science platform with broad impact in quantum simulation, quantum computation, and quantum metrology. The polarization dependence of anisotropic vector and tensor light shifts offers a degree of freedom for precise quantum state engineering of trapped particles. Similarly, state-selective operations depend on the polarization of the addressing light through the atom--light coupling strength. Yet, methods for controlling the polarization of individual tweezers or local addressing beams remain an experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate independent, site-resolved linear polarization rotation across an optical tweezer array by exploiting the local birefringence tunability of a spatial light modulator. Applying this capability to an array of $^{88}\rm{Sr}$ atoms, we homogenize differential light shifts imparted by the 813-nm tweezers to the narrow ${^1{\rm S}_0}\leftrightarrow{^3{\rm P}_1}$ transition, enabling sideband cooling under a magic-angle condition. Furthermore, we show dynamic transport of trapped atoms across distinct polarization zones with high survival and preserved coherence. Finally, we characterize tweezer polarization noise and demonstrate closed-loop stabilization referenced to the atomic transition frequency, reaching mrad-level stability. Our work establishes a technique for manipulating polarization-sensitive atomic and molecular transitions in tweezer architectures, with immediate applications to optical tweezer clocks and multi-zone quantum processors.

AI.tldr: Demo of independent, site-resolved linear polarization rotation across an optical tweezer array using a spatial light modulator's local birefringence, applied to trapped 88Sr atoms for light-shift homogenization, sideband cooling, polarization-zone transport, and mrad-level polarization stabilization.
AI.motivation: Polarization of trapping and addressing light governs anisotropic vector/tensor light shifts and state-selective atom-light coupling, but controlling polarization of individual tweezers or local addressing beams independently remains an experimental challenge.
AI.method: Exploit local birefringence tunability of a spatial light modulator to perform independent, site-resolved linear polarization rotation across an optical tweezer array; apply to a 88Sr array to homogenize differential light shifts from 813-nm tweezers on the narrow 1S0-3P1 transition and to implement sideband cooling under a magic-angle condition. Also demonstrate dynamic transport across distinct polarization zones and closed-loop polarization stabilization referenced to the atomic transition frequency.
AI.result: Homogenized differential light shifts enabling sideband cooling; dynamic transport across polarization zones with high survival and preserved coherence; characterization of tweezer polarization noise and closed-loop stabilization reaching mrad-level stability.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a technique for manipulating polarization-sensitive atomic and molecular transitions in tweezer architectures, with immediate applications to optical tweezer clocks and multi-zone quantum processors.

title: Ceramic Materials: From Atomic Bonding and Processing to Microstructure, Functional Properties, and Biomedical Applications
summary: Ceramic materials are inorganic, predominantly nonmetallic solids whose performance is governed by the interplay among atomic bonding, crystal structure, processing, microstructure, and functional properties. Their ionic and covalent bonding provides high hardness, thermal and chemical stability, wear resistance, and diverse electrical behavior, but also limits plastic deformation and increases sensitivity to flaws, porosity, grain boundaries, and residual stresses. This review examines ceramics through the processing--microstructure--property--performance relationship, emphasizing the effects of crystal chemistry, defects, grain size, porosity, and phase stability on mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biological behavior. Conventional sintering, sol--gel processing, and additive manufacturing are discussed as key routes for controlling densification, porosity, geometry, and composition. Biomedical ceramics, including alumina, zirconia, calcium phosphates, hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, and bioactive glasses, are also reviewed. Emerging topics include nanoceramics, smart ceramics, composites, multimaterial manufacturing, defect engineering, immunomodulatory bioceramics, and sustainable processing. Major challenges remain in brittle fracture, processing heterogeneity, degradation control, scale-up, and the porosity--strength trade-off. Future advances will require integrating advanced manufacturing, multiscale characterization, predictive modeling, and data-driven design.

AI.tldr: This review frames ceramics through the processing–microstructure–property–performance relationship, covering bonding, defects, sintering/sol–gel/additive manufacturing, and biomedical ceramics, while outlining challenges such as brittleness and the porosity–strength trade-off and future directions in advanced manufacturing and data-driven design.
AI.motivation: Ceramics possess attractive properties (hardness, thermal/chemical stability, wear resistance, diverse electrical behavior) arising from ionic and covalent bonding, yet the same bonding limits plastic deformation and makes performance highly sensitive to flaws, porosity, grain boundaries, and residual stresses. A coherent framework is needed to understand and control this structure–property sensitivity across conventional and emerging ceramic systems.
AI.method: A review approach organized around the processing–microstructure–property–performance relationship. It analyzes the effects of crystal chemistry, defects, grain size, porosity, and phase stability on mechanical, thermal, electrical, and biological behavior, and surveys processing routes including conventional sintering, sol–gel processing, and additive manufacturing for controlling densification, porosity, geometry, and composition. Biomedical ceramics (alumina, zirconia, calcium phosphates, hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, bioactive glasses) are also examined.
AI.result: The review consolidates how bonding, defects, and microstructural features govern ceramic performance, and identifies emerging topics: nanoceramics, smart ceramics, composites, multimaterial manufacturing, defect engineering, immunomodulatory bioceramics, and sustainable processing. It highlights persistent challenges in brittle fracture, processing heterogeneity, degradation control, scale-up, and the porosity–strength trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Progress in ceramics will require integrating advanced manufacturing, multiscale characterization, predictive modeling, and data-driven design to overcome brittleness, processing variability, degradation, scale-up barriers, and the porosity–strength trade-off.

title: Controlling transitions between nonequilibrium states through active bath engineering
summary: We develop a family of control protocols for finite-time transitions between active nonequilibrium steady states using the noise-color (correlation rate) as the sole control parameter. By reverse-engineering the second moment dynamics of an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, we determine the time-dependent correlation rate required to realize a prescribed evolution of the system's state. We experimentally implement these protocols with a micrometer-sized optically trapped particle coupled to an engineered active bath, demonstrating transitions substantially faster than the natural relaxation while keeping the confining potential, noise amplitude, and temperature fixed. Our approach extends engineered swift-equilibration methods to far-from-equilibrium steady states by directly controlling the temporal correlations of an active environment. We show how physical constraints impose a speed limit on finite-time transitions, while the freedom in choosing the prescribed system evolution can be exploited to eliminate control discontinuities, minimize the admissible transition time, or optimize a thermodynamic cost.

AI.tldr: The authors develop and experimentally demonstrate control protocols that achieve fast finite-time transitions between active nonequilibrium steady states by using the noise correlation rate (noise color) as the sole control parameter, extending swift-equilibration methods to far-from-equilibrium states.
AI.motivation: Swift-equilibration (finite-time control) methods have been established for equilibrium systems, but extending them to active, far-from-equilibrium steady states remains an open challenge. The authors aim to control active nonequilibrium steady states without altering the confining potential, noise amplitude, or temperature.
AI.method: They reverse-engineer the second-moment dynamics of an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process to determine the time-dependent correlation rate needed to realize a prescribed state evolution. These protocols are implemented experimentally with a micrometer-sized optically trapped particle coupled to an engineered active bath, controlling only the temporal correlations (noise color) of the active environment.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrate transitions between active nonequilibrium steady states substantially faster than the natural relaxation, while keeping the confining potential, noise amplitude, and temperature fixed. Physical constraints are shown to impose a speed limit on finite-time transitions.
AI.conclusion: The freedom in choosing the prescribed system evolution can be exploited to eliminate control discontinuities, minimize the admissible transition time, or optimize a thermodynamic cost. The approach generalizes engineered swift-equilibration to far-from-equilibrium steady states by directly controlling the temporal correlations of an active bath.

title: Isotope Effects at Classical Cost through Mass-Differentiable Machine Learning
summary: Isotope effects govern fractionation and modulate reactivity, with applications from hydrogen energy to environmental science and catalysis, yet predicting them requires resolving small isotope-dependent free-energy differences that remain very challenging for conventional path-integral simulations in complex systems. Here we introduce iso-EPIGS, a path-integral coarse-graining framework built on a mass-differentiable neural network that reconstructs the mass- and temperature-dependent path integral centroid free-energy surface. Classical molecular dynamics on the learned surface yields rigorous isotope-resolved thermodynamics without explicit path-integral sampling. Benchmarks spanning gas, liquid, and crystalline phases, including liquid water and oxalic acid crystal, reproduce reference path-integral isotope free-energy differences, enthalpies, and lattice parameters at near classical computational cost. Crucially, iso-EPIGS trained solely on all-H and all-D isotopologues retains high accuracy for unseen partially deuterated isotopologues, demonstrating robust transferability across nuclear masses. Iso-EPIGS makes accurate isotope-effect simulations feasible for complex systems and lays the groundwork for foundation models of isotope effects across chemical space.

AI.tldr: iso-EPIGS: a path-integral coarse-graining framework using a mass-differentiable neural network to reconstruct mass/temperature-dependent path integral centroid free-energy surfaces, enabling isotope-resolved thermodynamics at near-classical cost without explicit path-integral sampling.
AI.motivation: Isotope effects govern fractionation and modulate reactivity across hydrogen energy, environmental science, and catalysis, but predicting them requires resolving small isotope-dependent free-energy differences. Conventional path-integral simulations struggle with these tiny differences in complex systems.
AI.method: iso-EPIGS builds a mass-differentiable neural network that reconstructs the mass- and temperature-dependent path integral centroid free-energy surface, on which classical molecular dynamics yields rigorous isotope-resolved thermodynamics without explicit path-integral sampling.
AI.result: Benchmarks across gas, liquid, and crystalline phases (liquid water, oxalic acid crystal) reproduce reference path-integral isotope free-energy differences, enthalpies, and lattice parameters at near-classical cost. Models trained solely on all-H and all-D isotopologues retain high accuracy for unseen partially deuterated isotopologues, showing transferability across nuclear masses.
AI.conclusion: iso-EPIGS makes accurate isotope-effect simulations feasible for complex systems and provides groundwork for foundation models of isotope effects across chemical space.

title: Can end-to-end learning from raw electronic structure explain magnetic anisotropy?
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables, Supporting Information included
summary: Machine-learning models trained directly on electronic spectra can predict spin--orbit-driven properties, yet models with comparable predictive accuracy may learn different electronic dependencies. We examine this problem using magnetic anisotropy in atomic-scale magnets and a validation strategy designed to assess the physical relevance of learned spectral relationships. We compare a bidirectional gated recurrent unit and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network, both trained to predict magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) from spin- and orbital-resolved scalar-relativistic densities of states (SR-DOS). Despite comparable in-domain (ID) accuracy, the architectures learn only partly overlapping spectral dependencies. Shapley additive explanations identify spectral features shared between the two architectures that can be associated with plausible spin--orbit-coupling pathways consistent with second-order perturbation theory (PT2). Adding PT2-derived MAE contributions to the model inputs has little effect on ID performance but can improve transfer beyond the training domain, with gains differing between architectures. Controlled spectral perturbations further demonstrate that similar attribution patterns do not imply the same functional dependence of the predicted MAE on spectral weight. The contrasting responses provide a functional context for architecture-dependent out-of-domain transfer. End-to-end learning can identify candidate electronic signatures of magnetic anisotropy. Their credible microscopic interpretation, however, rests on convergent evidence from predictive performance, model comparison, physical theory, controlled spectral interventions, and evaluation under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: Two architectures predicting magnetic anisotropy energy from spin- and orbital-resolved densities of states achieve similar in-domain accuracy but learn only partly overlapping spectral dependencies. Convergent evidence from explanations, perturbation theory, controlled perturbations, and out-of-domain transfer is needed for physically credible interpretation.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning models trained directly on electronic spectra can predict spin-orbit-driven properties, but models with comparable predictive accuracy may learn different electronic dependencies. This raises the question of whether learned spectral relationships are physically meaningful or merely predictive artifacts. The authors use magnetic anisotropy in atomic-scale magnets as a test case and seek a validation strategy to assess the physical relevance of learned spectral relationships.
AI.method: They compare a bidirectional gated recurrent unit (BiGRU) and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN), both trained to predict magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) from spin- and orbital-resolved scalar-relativistic densities of states (SR-DOS). They apply Shapley additive explanations to identify spectral features, relate them to spin-orbit-coupling pathways consistent with second-order perturbation theory (PT2), augment model inputs with PT2-derived MAE contributions, and perform controlled spectral perturbations to probe functional dependence, alongside out-of-domain transfer evaluation.
AI.result: Despite comparable in-domain (ID) accuracy, the two architectures learn only partly overlapping spectral dependencies. Shapley additive explanations identify shared spectral features associated with plausible spin-orbit-coupling pathways consistent with PT2. Adding PT2-derived MAE contributions has little effect on ID performance but can improve transfer beyond the training domain, with gains differing between architectures. Controlled spectral perturbations show that similar attribution patterns do not imply the same functional dependence of predicted MAE on spectral weight, providing a functional context for architecture-dependent out-of-domain transfer.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end learning can identify candidate electronic signatures of magnetic anisotropy. Their credible microscopic interpretation, however, rests on convergent evidence from predictive performance, model comparison, physical theory, controlled spectral interventions, and evaluation under distribution shift. Comparable predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to establish physical relevance.

title: Robust skyrmion nucleation and transport via composition gradient in rare earth-transition metal ferrimagnets
summary: Magnetic skyrmions are typically nucleated via localized excitation methods, such as laser heating, spin-orbit torques, or engineered defects, and their controlled transport is often limited by the skyrmion Hall effect. Here, we demonstrate that spatial gradients in rare-earth--transition-metal alloys, achievable through patterned laser writing, enable both deterministic nucleation and controlled transport. The strategy leverages engineered compositional gradient to cross the magnetization compensation point, defining regions with opposite magnetization. An out-of-plane magnetic field selectively reverses the magnetization, generating a skyrmion. Crucially, the same compositional design enables a channel tuned to the spin angular momentum compensation point, where skyrmions are driven by spin-orbit torques at high velocity with vanishing skyrmion Hall effect. Local composition variations act as pinning sites, enabling threshold-controlled trapping and release.

AI.tldr: Spatial compositional gradients in rare-earth–transition-metal (RE-TM) alloys created by patterned laser writing enable deterministic magnetic skyrmion nucleation and controlled transport, including high-velocity motion with vanishing skyrmion Hall effect and threshold-controlled pinning/depinning.
AI.motivation: Conventional skyrmion nucleation relies on localized excitation methods (laser heating, spin-orbit torques, engineered defects), and controlled transport is typically hindered by the skyrmion Hall effect, limiting deterministic and efficient skyrmion manipulation.
AI.method: Engineered spatial compositional gradients in RE-TM alloys via patterned laser writing. The gradient crosses the magnetization compensation point, defining regions of opposite magnetization. An out-of-plane magnetic field selectively reverses magnetization to nucleate a skyrmion. The same compositional design provides a channel tuned to the spin angular momentum compensation point. Local composition variations serve as pinning sites for threshold-controlled trapping and release.
AI.result: Deterministic skyrmion nucleation is achieved. Skyrmions are driven by spin-orbit torques at high velocity with a vanishing skyrmion Hall effect within the tuned channel. Local composition variations enable threshold-controlled trapping and release.
AI.conclusion: Compositional gradients in RE-TM alloys, readily created by patterned laser writing, offer a versatile route for simultaneous deterministic skyrmion nucleation, high-velocity Hall-effect-free transport, and threshold-controlled pinning/release.

title: EPR as a probe for the mechanisms of chirality-induced spin selectivity in photoinduced charge transfer
summary: Several models for chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) in charge transfer have been proposed, but rarely compared directly with experiments. This step is essential for their validation and future progress of the field. Here we investigate a broad class of radical pair states associated with different microscopic models by computing the related electron-paramagnetic resonance spectra. This allows us to evidence peculiar signatures of different radical pair states, to study their experimental accessibility and identify conditions to verify proposed microscopic models.

AI.tldr: The authors compute EPR spectra for a broad class of radical pair states tied to different microscopic CISS models to reveal distinctive signatures, assess experimental accessibility, and identify conditions for validating the proposed models.
AI.motivation: Many microscopic models for chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) in charge transfer exist, but they are rarely tested directly against experiments. Such comparison is essential for validating these models and advancing the field.
AI.method: The study investigates a broad class of radical pair states corresponding to different microscopic models and computes their associated electron-paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra.
AI.result: The computed EPR spectra reveal peculiar signatures characteristic of different radical pair states, allowing assessment of their experimental accessibility.
AI.conclusion: EPR spectroscopy provides identifiable signatures that can be used to verify proposed microscopic CISS models and identify conditions under which such verification is feasible.

title: Displacement-Field-Induced Ionization of Defect States in High-Quality hBN
summary: Encapsulation of two-dimensional (2D) materials with hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is widely used to fabricate ultraclean van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures for optoelectronic and quantum transport studies. These devices are often operated under strong out-of-plane displacement fields that tune the electronic properties of the active 2D material, while the surrounding hBN is typically assumed to remain electronically inert. This assumption, however, neglects defect states that are present even in high-quality hBN crystals. Here, we probe their response to the applied displacement field using monolayer graphene encapsulated between hBN crystals as a sensitive charge sensor. Increasing the displacement field induces notable charge transfer between graphene and hBN, producing additional electron doping of 10-20x10^9 cm^(-2) even at the moderate displacement field (~0.5 V nm^(-1)), while simultaneously increasing carrier-density inhomogeneity of the graphene layer. Both effects are consistent with ionization of defect states within the hBN bandgap, with the bulk density ~1-7x10^(-5) nm^(-3) varying across different hBN crystals. Our results show that displacement-field-induced defect ionization in hBN can modify the electronic response of vdW heterostructures, with direct implications for device design and interpretation of experiments.

This assumption ignores defect states present even in high-quality hBN crystals, so their response to the applied displacement field is unknown.

Both effects are consistent with ionization of defect states within the hBN bandgap, with a bulk density of ~1-7x10^(-5) nm^(-3) that varies across different hBN crystals.

title: Strain-engineered long-distance supercurrent in an altermagnetic CrSb based-Josephson junction
summary: Altermagnetic materials, characterized by vanishing net magnetization and momentum-dependent spin splitting, provide a unique platform for realizing unconventional superconducting states without the detrimental stray fields. Here, we demonstrate long-distance Josephson supercurrent transport through epitaxial thin films of the strained altermagnet CrSb. We observe a dissipationless supercurrent across a lateral spacer distance of 150 nm in a CrSb-based Josephson junction, exceeding the conventional spin-singlet coherence length by nearly two orders of magnitude. This supercurrent is further accompanied by a well-defined magnetic-field-induced quantum interference pattern, providing direct evidence for genuine Josephson coupling. Our results reveal altermagnets as a promising route toward generating long-distance supercurrents without macroscopic magnetic stray fields, opening new opportunities for superconducting spintronic applications.

AI.tldr: Long-distance dissipationless Josephson supercurrent with quantum interference is demonstrated through a 150 nm strained altermagnet CrSb spacer, far exceeding the spin-singlet coherence length.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets combine vanishing net magnetization with momentum-dependent spin splitting, enabling unconventional superconducting states free of stray fields. However, realizing long-distance supercurrent transport through altermagnetic spacers remains a key open challenge.
AI.method: Epitaxial thin films of strained altermagnet CrSb were integrated into lateral Josephson junctions, and supercurrent transport was measured across spacers up to 150 nm, complemented by magnetic-field-dependent interference measurements.
AI.result: A dissipationless supercurrent is observed across a 150 nm lateral spacer, exceeding the conventional spin-singlet coherence length by nearly two orders of magnitude. A well-defined magnetic-field-induced quantum interference pattern confirms genuine Josephson coupling.
AI.conclusion: Altermagnets offer a promising route to long-distance supercurrents without macroscopic magnetic stray fields, opening new opportunities for superconducting spintronic applications.

title: Competing symmetry breaking and topology in quantum spin chains
summary: We investigate how spontaneous symmetry breaking and symmetry-protected topology compete and cooperate in one-dimensional quantum spin-1/2 systems. We introduce two families of local Hamiltonians with $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{T}_{2}$ symmetry which host a zoo of broken-symmetry phases with and without gapless boundary spins, namely, six long-range-ordered gapped phases that differ by their $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}$-symmetry-breaking patterns (FM$^{\,}_{x,y,z}$ and Neel$^{\,}_{x,y,z}$), their partner symmetry-protected topological phases (FM$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{x,y}$ and Neel$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{x,y}$), and two gapless phases (gFM$^{\,}_{z}$ and gNeel$^{\,}_{z}$) with incommensurate $\mathbb{Z}^{T}_{2}$-breaking magnetic long-range order and central charge $\mathsf{c}=1$. Direct transitions between competing gapped phases can be continuous or weakly first order. We demonstrate that continuous phase transition lines have exotic critical properties. For example, a line of deconfined quantum critical points (between the Neel$^{\,}_{x}$ and Neel$^{\,}_{y}$ phases) described by Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory is terminated by the gFM$^{\,}_{z}$ phase at a Lifshitz tricritical point which exhibits spontaneous breaking of the continuous U(1) symmetry despite the locality and one-dimensionality of the Hamiltonian, contrary to a naive expectation from the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner-Coleman theorem. Furthermore, critical lines between symmetry-protected topological phases with different $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}$-symmetry breaking (e.g., Neel$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{x}$ and Neel$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{y}$) additionally retain low-energy boundary degrees of freedom, realizing symmetry-enriched criticality (or a gapless SPT phase). Our results reveal unconventional mechanisms by which competing symmetry breaking and topology generate ordered critical phases and multicriticality.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the interplay between spontaneous symmetry breaking and symmetry-protected topology in one-dimensional spin-1/2 systems with Z2×Z2×Z2^T symmetry, revealing a rich phase diagram with gapped ordered phases, their SPT partners, and gapless phases, connected by exotic continuous and weakly first-order transitions including deconfined quantum criticality and symmetry-enriched criticality.
AI.motivation: Understanding how spontaneous symmetry breaking and symmetry-protected topology compete and cooperate is a central question in quantum many-body physics. One-dimensional systems offer a tractable setting to explore this interplay, yet the full landscape of competing orders, topological phases, and their critical properties remains incompletely characterized.
AI.method: The authors introduce two families of local Hamiltonians with Z2×Z2×Z2^T symmetry for one-dimensional spin-1/2 systems. They systematically analyze the resulting phase diagram, characterize the gapped long-range-ordered phases (FM and Neel with different symmetry-breaking patterns), their symmetry-protected topological partners, and gapless phases with incommensurate magnetic long-range order (central charge c=1). They examine the nature of transitions between these phases, including deconfined quantum critical points described by Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, Lifshitz tricriticality, and symmetry-enriched criticality.
AI.result: The model hosts six gapped long-range-ordered phases (FM_{x,y,z}, Neel_{x,y,z}) differing by Z2-symmetry-breaking patterns, their SPT partners (FM^{SPT}_{x,y}, Neel^{SPT}_{x,y}), and two gapless phases (gFM_z, gNeel_z) with incommensurate Z2^T-breaking order and central charge c=1. Transitions between competing gapped phases can be continuous or weakly first order. A line of deconfined quantum critical points between Neel_x and Neel_y (Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid) terminates at a Lifshitz tricritical point where spontaneous U(1) symmetry breaking occurs. Critical lines between SPT phases with different Z2-symmetry breaking retain low-energy boundary degrees of freedom, realizing symmetry-enriched criticality.
AI.conclusion: Competing symmetry breaking and topology generate unconventional ordered critical phases and multicriticality. The Lifshitz tricritical point exhibits spontaneous continuous U(1) symmetry breaking despite one-dimensionality, apparently circumventing the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner-Coleman theorem. Critical lines between SPT phases realize symmetry-enriched criticality (gapless SPT phases), demonstrating that topology enriches quantum criticality in one dimension.

title: Data driven screening of CaCu$_5$-type magnetic structures
summary: We develop a machine learning assisted workflow for the rapid screening of permanent magnet candidates within the CaCu$_5$ structure family. We generated more than 60,000 structures through substitutions. These compositions were screened using a combination of pretrained materials models, Materials Project data, and a machine-learning model for magnetization prediction. Four criteria, namely, metallicity, negative formation energy, energy above the convex hull $\leq 50$~meV/atom, and predicted magnetization above the adopted $\geq 0.75$~T threshold reduced the initial chemical space to 439 candidates for first-principles calculations. Density functional theory calculations revealed that 159 compounds exhibit positive axial magnetic anisotropy energy, favoring [001] over the tested in-plane directions. The resulting dataset reveals chemical trends in magnetic anisotropy across the CaCu$_5$ compositional space and provides a set of candidates for further investigation. More broadly, this work demonstrates a practical strategy for combining existing machine learning models with first-principles calculations to systematically reduce large chemical spaces to tractable sets for computationally intensive materials screening.

AI.tldr: A machine learning plus DFT workflow screens >60,000 CaCu5-type substitutions, narrowing to 439 candidates and identifying 159 compounds with positive axial magnetic anisotropy favoring [001].
AI.motivation: Rapid discovery of permanent magnet candidates is limited by the vast chemical space and the cost of first-principles calculations. The CaCu5 structure family is a promising but underexplored compositional space, requiring an efficient screening strategy.
AI.method: Substitutional generation of >60,000 CaCu5-type structures. Screening via pretrained materials models, Materials Project data, and a machine-learning magnetization predictor, applying four filters: metallicity, negative formation energy, energy above convex hull <= 50 meV/atom, and predicted magnetization >= 0.75 T. DFT validation on 439 candidates with magnetic anisotropy energy evaluation comparing [001] against tested in-plane directions.
AI.result: 439 candidates entered DFT; 159 compounds show positive axial magnetic anisotropy energy favoring [001]. The dataset reveals chemical trends in magnetic anisotropy across the CaCu5 compositional space.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a tractable candidate set for further permanent magnet investigation and demonstrates a practical, generalizable strategy of combining pretrained ML models with first-principles calculations to reduce large chemical spaces for intensive materials screening.

title: The Fiedler dimension of networks of networks: from fractal to small-world architectures
summary: Is the relaxation of a modular network dictated by its modules or by the network that connects them? The answer fixes the time scales of diffusion, consensus, and synchronization, all set by the Fiedler eigenvalue. We show that, for bundled networks, the two levels act one after the other: a random walker must first escape from its module and then spread over the network that connects them. The equilibration time is the sum of these two times, the time needed to reach the base from inside a fiber and the relaxation time of the base, slowed down by the mass of the fibers. The consequences are unexpected. However large the modules are, a small-world core always imposes its own Fiedler dimension; the modules survive only as a logarithmic correction, which slows down equilibration and hides the true exponent up to sizes far beyond any real network. Effective dimensions measured on finite modular systems can therefore be systematically biased. We analytically work out all combinations of finite-dimensional and small-world bases and fibers, and compare them with numerically exact spectra of representatives of each category.

AI.tldr: The relaxation/equilibration time of bundled modular networks equals the sum of two sequential processes—escape from a module plus spreading over the connecting network—so that a small-world core imposes its Fiedler dimension even for arbitrarily large modules, with modules surviving only as a logarithmic correction that can systematically bias measured effective dimensions.
AI.motivation: Relaxation of modular networks is governed by the Fiedler eigenvalue, which fixes the time scales of diffusion, consensus, and synchronization. The open question is whether this relaxation is dictated by the modules themselves or by the network connecting them, and clarifying this has direct consequences for interpreting dynamics and for dimension measurements on modular systems.
AI.method: The authors analyze "bundled" networks (a base connecting fibers/modules) and show that the two structural levels act sequentially. They derive the equilibration time as the sum of two contributions: the time to reach the base from inside a fiber, and the relaxation time of the base slowed down by the mass of the fibers. They analytically treat all combinations of finite-dimensional and small-world bases and fibers, and compare these predictions with numerically exact spectra of representative networks from each category.
AI.result: Relaxation is sequential: a random walker first escapes its module, then spreads over the connecting network. However large the modules are, a small-world core imposes its own Fiedler dimension; the modules persist only as a logarithmic correction, which slows equilibration and hides the true exponent up to sizes far beyond any real network.
AI.conclusion: The Fiedler eigenvalue—and thus diffusion, consensus, and synchronization time scales—of bundled modular networks is fixed by the Fiedler dimension of the connecting core rather than by the modules. Modules contribute only logarithmic corrections, so effective dimensions measured on finite modular systems can be systematically biased.

title: Non-Perturbative Vibrational Excitation by Arbitrary Electric Fields from Classical Phase-Space Dynamics
summary: We present a non-perturbative framework for the quantum treatment of vibrational excitation in molecular systems driven by electric fields with arbitrary time dependence. For harmonic potentials with linear dipole coupling, the field-induced dynamics is exactly described by a displaced coherent state, whose evolution is completely determined by a complex phase-space coordinate. Closed-form expressions for this coordinate reveal a clear distinction between resonant and non-resonant regimes. The resulting vibrational populations follow a Poisson distribution determined by a dimensionless time-dependent phase-space displacement, for both resonant and non-resonant driving. Resonant driving results in an enhanced phase-space displacement, whereas finite detuning between the driving and vibrational frequencies leads to an exponential suppression of the phase-space displacement and vibrational excitation. While the approach reduces to the standard time-dependent perturbation theory in the weak-field limit, it remains valid in the strong-field regime, where perturbative treatments fail. Our results provide a transparent phase-space picture of vibrational control and enable non-perturbative state preparation in ultrafast spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: A non-perturbative phase-space framework exactly describes field-driven vibrational dynamics of harmonic oscillators via a displaced coherent state, with Poisson-distributed populations valid from weak to strong fields.
AI.motivation: Perturbative treatments break down for strong-field vibrational excitation, so a non-perturbative description is needed for molecular systems driven by arbitrarily time-dependent electric fields.
AI.method: For harmonic potentials with linear dipole coupling, the field-induced dynamics is exactly represented by a displaced coherent state governed by a complex phase-space coordinate. Closed-form expressions for this coordinate are derived, distinguishing resonant and non-resonant regimes.
AI.result: Vibrational populations follow a Poisson distribution set by a dimensionless time-dependent phase-space displacement for both resonant and non-resonant driving. Resonant driving enhances the displacement, while detuning causes exponential suppression. The approach reduces to standard time-dependent perturbation theory in the weak-field limit but stays valid in the strong-field regime.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a transparent phase-space picture of vibrational control and enables non-perturbative state preparation in ultrafast spectroscopy.

title: Homogeneous Charge Relaxation in Organic Mixed Ionic-Electronic Conductors
summary: Organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs) couple ionic and electronic signals, enabling energy storage, neuromorphic computing, and bioelectronics. However, how charge relaxes in water once the bias is removed, which determines how long stored states persist, remains unclear. Using operando charge photometry, we tracked charge in OMIEC films during biasing and open-circuit relaxation. Under bias, charges moved as redox fronts. After bias removal, charge instead relaxed uniformly across the channel. Modeling and cryo-electron microscopy indicate that swelling creates connected water-rich pathways through the bulk. These pathways speed ion motion but also let stored charge leak away. Tuning the terminal side chain of a polythiophene controls water uptake and ion trapping. Bulky hydrophobic side chains enable stable programmable states, whereas hydrophilic side chains support fast electrophysiology sensing.

AI.tldr: Using operando charge photometry, this work reveals that charge relaxation in OMIECs after bias removal is spatially uniform rather than front-like, driven by water-rich swelling pathways that enable fast ion transport but also cause charge leakage; side-chain engineering tunes this trade-off.
AI.motivation: OMIECs couple ionic and electronic signals, enabling energy storage, neuromorphic computing, and bioelectronics, but the mechanism by which charge relaxes in water once the bias is removed—determining how long stored states persist—remains unclear.
AI.method: Operando charge photometry tracked charge in OMIEC films during biasing and open-circuit relaxation; results were complemented by modeling and cryo-electron microscopy. Terminal side chains of a polythiophene were tuned to control water uptake and ion trapping.
AI.result: Under bias, charges moved as redox fronts; after bias removal, charge relaxed uniformly across the channel. Swelling creates connected water-rich pathways through the bulk that speed ion motion but also let stored charge leak away. Bulky hydrophobic side chains enable stable programmable states, whereas hydrophilic side chains support fast electrophysiology sensing.
AI.conclusion: Charge relaxation in OMIECs is governed by swelling-induced water-rich percolation pathways, establishing a design trade-off between state retention and ion-transport speed that can be tuned via terminal side-chain chemistry.

title: Reading Altermagnetic Domains with Photon Drag
summary: Finite photon momentum allows second-order photocurrents in centrosymmetric space groups, where the conventional bulk photovoltaic effect is forbidden. Here we study the photon-drag response of altermagnets and show that its angular dependence reveals both the symmetry of the magnetic order and the Néel domain of the sample. For example, when a crystal rotation exchanges the two domains, the domain-even and domain-odd parts of the current appear in different angular harmonics, $4n$ and $4n+2$ for tetragonal $d$-wave altermagnets, so that two measurements rotated by $90^\circ$ on a single domain isolate the domain-odd current. We also find that these microscopic contributions exhibit opposite domain parities depending on light polarization. Under linear light, only the shift term is domain odd, while under circular light, the domain-odd channel switches to the injection, Fermi-surface, and contact principal-value terms. Mirror symmetries fix the angular phase of each harmonic and distinguish $d_{x^2-y^2}$, $d_{xy}$, and $g$-wave order. In contrast, conventional collinear antiferromagnets show no domain-odd photon-drag current, and in tetragonal ferromagnets the two parts share the same harmonics. Although the altermagnetic spin splitting does not require spin-orbit coupling (SOC), SOC is essential to observe the domain-odd charge current. Our work uncovers distinct signatures of altermagnetism in photon drag and provides a route to all optical magnetic readouts of altermagnets.

AI.tldr: Photon-drag currents in altermagnets exhibit domain-odd and domain-even angular harmonics that probe magnetic order symmetry, Néel domain configuration, and order-parameter type ($d_{x^2-y^2}$, $d_{xy}$, $g$-wave), where SOC is required to observe the domain-odd charge current.
AI.motivation: Second-order (photon-drag) photocurrents arise from finite photon momentum even in centrosymmetric crystals where the conventional bulk photovoltaic effect is forbidden. The authors aim to determine whether the photon-drag response can serve as a symmetry-sensitive probe of altermagnetic order and its Néel domains, since altermagnets are centrosymmetric magnets with spin-split bands.
AI.method: The authors calculate the photon-drag response of altermagnets, decomposing it into domain-even and domain-odd contributions. They analyze the angular harmonics as a function of crystal rotation and light polarization (linear vs. circular), track the microscopic current terms (shift, injection, Fermi-surface, contact principal-value), and use mirror symmetries to fix angular phases. Comparisons are made to conventional collinear antiferromagnets and tetragonal ferromagnets.
AI.result: Domain-even and domain-odd currents appear in distinct angular harmonics ($4n$ and $4n+2$) for tetragonal $d$-wave altermagnets, so two measurements rotated by $90^\circ$ on a single domain isolate the domain-odd current. Microscopic contributions have opposite domain parities depending on polarization: under linear light only the shift term is domain odd; under circular light the domain-odd channel switches to injection, Fermi-surface, and contact principal-value terms. Mirror symmetries fix the angular phase, distinguishing $d_{x^2-y^2}$, $d_{xy}$, and $g$-wave order. Collinear antiferromagnets show no domain-odd photon-drag current, and tetragonal ferromagnets share the same harmonics for both parts. SOC is essential for the domain-odd charge current despite not being needed for the altermagnetic spin splitting.
AI.conclusion: Photon drag provides distinct symmetry signatures of altermagnetism and enables an all-optical magnetic readout of altermagnets, including identification of the magnetic order symmetry and Néel domain state.

title: From band reconstruction to Bogoliubov dispersion: How dz2-band enhances iron-based superconductivity
summary: Conventional understanding of iron-based superconductivity is usually established based on electronic bands at the Fermi level, leaving deeper bands overlooked as potential factor. Here, we expand this view by demonstrating that a deep-lying dz2 band below the Fermi level can be employed to enhance the superconducting paring strength. By using scanning tunneling microscope to mechanically change the crystal lattice of an iron-based superconductor, we observe an upward shift of the deep-lying dz2 band related feature, leading to hybridization with the primary superconducting bands at the Fermi level. We visualize the novel evidence of this band hybridization and resulting enhanced superconducting gap through quasiparticle interference imaging, providing conclusive evidence that engineering such correlations between deep and pairing-active bands is a potent mechanism for amplifying the superconducting gap. This work refines the conventional view of pairing-relevant electronic structures and establishes band hybridization as an effective way to optimize superconducting materials.

AI.tldr: A deep-lying dz2 band below the Fermi level can be shifted upward via mechanical lattice modification to hybridize with the primary Fermi-level superconducting bands, thereby enhancing the superconducting pairing strength and gap in an iron-based superconductor.
AI.motivation: Conventional understanding of iron-based superconductivity is typically based solely on electronic bands at the Fermi level, leaving deeper bands overlooked as potential factors. This work aims to expand this view by testing whether a deep-lying dz2 band can be used to enhance superconducting pairing strength.
AI.method: Scanning tunneling microscope (STM) was used to mechanically modify the crystal lattice of an iron-based superconductor. Quasiparticle interference (QPI) imaging was employed to visualize the band hybridization and the resulting superconducting gap.
AI.result: Mechanical lattice modification caused an upward shift of the deep-lying dz2 band related feature, leading to hybridization with the primary superconducting bands at the Fermi level. QPI imaging provided direct evidence of this band hybridization and the associated enhanced superconducting gap.
AI.conclusion: Engineering correlations between deep bands and pairing-active bands is a potent mechanism for amplifying the superconducting gap. This work refines the conventional view of pairing-relevant electronic structures and establishes band hybridization as an effective route to optimize superconducting materials.

title: Symmetric Mode Ansatz: Theory of Magnon Collective Modes in Chern Insulators
summary: Moiré materials host integer and fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) where time-reversal is broken spontaneously by flat band ferromagnetism. In twisted MoTe2, unlike in quantum Hall, opposite spins carry opposite Chern numbers and realize Ising ferromagnetism with gapped magnon excitations. Clarifying the nature of these collective modes and the origin of the magnon gap is key to understanding the stability of the Chern magnets in these materials. To do so, we develop a generalized single-mode approximation, which we call the symmetric mode ansatz (SyMA), to describe the low-energy magnon spectrum. We find it to be in exceptional agreement with numerical calculations at integer filling, and qualitatively accurate across fractional fillings including FCIs. To explain the accuracy of the SyMA, we present two families of Hubbard models (including the Haldane model and continuum ideal bands) whose collective modes are analytically solvable and for which the SyMA is either exact or an accurate approximation. For a class of these models where SyMA is exact, we prove two-sided bounds on the zero-momentum magnon gap in terms of the Chern number, Berry curvature, and quantum metric, revealing that uniform quantum geometry is sufficient for stabilizing magnetism in Chern bands.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a symmetric mode ansatz (SyMA), a generalized single-mode approximation, to describe low-energy magnon spectra in moiré Chern magnets, showing excellent agreement with numerics and proving two-sided bounds on the magnon gap in terms of Chern number, Berry curvature, and quantum metric.
AI.motivation: In twisted MoTe2, opposite spins carry opposite Chern numbers, realizing Ising ferromagnetism with gapped magnons. Clarifying the nature of these collective modes and the origin of the magnon gap is essential to understanding the stability of Chern magnets in these materials.
AI.method: The authors develop a generalized single-mode approximation called the symmetric mode ansatz (SyMA) to describe the low-energy magnon spectrum. They validate it against numerical calculations at integer filling and across fractional fillings including FCIs. They also present two families of Hubbard models with analytically solvable collective modes for which SyMA is exact or an accurate approximation.
AI.result: SyMA shows exceptional agreement with numerical calculations at integer filling and qualitative accuracy across fractional fillings including FCIs. For models where SyMA is exact, the authors prove two-sided bounds on the zero-momentum magnon gap in terms of Chern number, Berry curvature, and quantum metric.
AI.conclusion: Uniform quantum geometry is sufficient for stabilizing magnetism in Chern bands, providing a theoretical basis for the stability of Chern magnets in moiré materials.

title: Band Tail States: Speed Bump or End of the Road for Two-Dimensional Semiconductors?
summary: We propose that the path to realizing the full potential of two-dimensional (2D) electronics lies in understanding and mastering their energy band tail states (BTS). Unlike silicon, which benefits from sharp band edges (Urbach energy $E_\rm U$ ~ 10 meV), today's monolayer 2D semiconductors have rough band edges ($E_\rm U$ ~ 100 meV) caused by spatial potential inhomogeneity. Comparing a physics-based electrical model to experiments, we demonstrate that BTS cause reduced effective mobility and "slow" transistor turn-on with excessive gate voltage in monolayer 2D transistors, which sets a fundamental limit for their energy-efficient operation. We also show that BTS effects in 2D transistors could be mitigated with higher gate capacitance, with strain engineering, and by using bilayer instead of monolayer 2D channels, as long as $E_\rm U$ is reduced below ~ 50 meV. This work provides a theoretical framework and design guidelines to navigate these fundamental limits, and to enable successful integration of 2D semiconductors into low-power nanoelectronics.

AI.tldr: Band tail states (BTS) arising from spatial potential inhomogeneity in monolayer 2D semiconductors (Urbach energy ~100 meV vs ~10 meV in Si) fundamentally limit the energy-efficient operation of 2D transistors; the authors propose mitigation strategies to reduce BTS effects.
AI.motivation: To realize the full potential of 2D electronics, it is essential to understand and master the energy band tail states that degrade device performance. Unlike silicon with sharp band edges, today's monolayer 2D semiconductors have rough band edges, imposing a fundamental limit on energy-efficient operation that must be addressed for low-power nanoelectronics.
AI.method: A physics-based electrical model is compared against experiments to quantify the impact of BTS in monolayer 2D transistors. Mitigation approaches examined include increasing gate capacitance, applying strain engineering, and replacing monolayer with bilayer 2D channels.
AI.result: BTS reduce effective mobility and cause "slow" transistor turn-on requiring excessive gate voltage. BTS effects can be mitigated via higher gate capacitance, strain engineering, and bilayer channels, provided the Urbach energy is reduced below ~50 meV.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework and design guidelines to navigate the fundamental limits imposed by BTS, enabling successful integration of 2D semiconductors into low-power nanoelectronics.

title: Mutual Linearity of Complexes in Chemical Reaction Networks
summary: Exact statements about how a system far from equilibrium responds to changes in its rate constants are scarce beyond linear response, yet they are central to the control of biochemical networks. A notable exception is mutual linearity: in a jump process, controlling the rates of a single transition makes any two stationary probabilities obey an exact affine relation, arbitrarily far from equilibrium. With nonlinear mass-action kinetics, and conservation laws in place of a normalization, chemical reaction networks seem to defy mutual linearity since species concentrations obey no such relation. We show that it was there all along, in the complexes' activities (mass-action monomials) rather than in the concentrations of species. For zero-deficiency networks with a single linkage class, controlling one reaction makes any three stationary activities obey a linear relation whose coefficients are independent of the controlled rate constants, the conserved quantities (hence the initial state), and even of the stoichiometry of complexes. This predicts hidden activities and bounds the activity ratios the control can reach, while a violation signals nonzero deficiency or multiple linkage classes.

AI.tldr: The paper extends "mutual linearity" from jump processes to nonlinear mass-action chemical reaction networks, showing that an exact linear relation holds among stationary complex activities (not species concentrations) when one reaction rate is varied, for zero-deficiency networks with a single linkage class.
AI.motivation: Exact statements about how far-from-equilibrium systems respond to changes in rate constants are scarce beyond linear response, yet such statements are essential for controlling biochemical networks. Mutual linearity is a known exception for jump processes, but chemical reaction networks with nonlinear mass-action kinetics and conservation laws appear to violate it because species concentrations obey no such relation. The authors aim to recover an analogous exact relation for CRNs.
AI.method: The authors shift attention from species concentrations to complexes' activities (the mass-action monomials). By controlling one reaction's rate constant in a mass-action chemical reaction network, they derive an exact affine/linear relation among stationary complex activities, exploiting the structure of zero-deficiency networks with a single linkage class.
AI.result: For zero-deficiency networks with a single linkage class, controlling one reaction makes any three stationary activities obey a linear relation whose coefficients are independent of the controlled rate constants, the conserved quantities (hence the initial state), and even of the stoichiometry of the complexes. The result predicts hidden activities and bounds the activity ratios reachable by the control. A violation of the relation signals nonzero deficiency or multiple linkage classes.
AI.conclusion: Mutual linearity is preserved in chemical reaction networks once expressed in terms of complex activities rather than species concentrations, providing an exact far-from-equilibrium control law and a diagnostic for network structure (deficiency and linkage classes).

title: Predictable Accuracy of Martini 3 Absolute Protein-Ligand Binding Free Energies across 15 Targets
summary: Alchemical free-energy calculations predict protein-ligand binding affinities with close-to-experimental accuracy, but their cost restricts them to small sets of ligands. Coarse-grained (CG) models such as Martini 3 retain a rigorous statistical-mechanical treatment at a fraction of this cost, yet their accuracy for protein-ligand binding has not been assessed systematically. Here, we compute absolute binding free energies for 172 ligands across 15 protein targets with a Martini 3 double-decoupling protocol and compare them against atomistic FEP+ and OpenFE references. Martini underbinds for every target, by 2.7 to 8.7 kcal/mol. This offset is systematic: it comprises a uniform contribution that grows with the number of charged pocket residues. A linear model in this number, which requires only the protein structure, reduces the mean absolute error from 5.7 to 1.2 kcal/mol in leave-one-out cross-validation, close to the 1.0 kcal/mol obtained with exact per-target offsets. The ranking of ligands within a target varies more widely (median Spearman $ρ$ of 0.32, from $-$0.41 to 0.89) and is rationalized by the structure-activity relationship of each series: Martini ranks ligands well when their affinity is driven by hydrophobicity, $π$-stacking, or size, and poorly when it is driven by hydrogen bonding or charge. Both trends follow from Martini's calibration against bulk partitioning, which captures neither the dielectric environment of a binding pocket nor the directionality of hydrogen bonds. While MMGBSA retains the atomistic detail needed to rank congeneric ligands, Martini yields physically meaningful free energies, and its coarse-graining maps many atomistically distinct molecules onto one representation, making it a complementary tool for rapidly spanning chemical space.

AI.tldr: Martini 3 coarse-grained absolute binding free energies for 172 ligands across 15 targets are systematically offset (underbinding by 2.7–8.7 kcal/mol) but correctable by a structure-based linear model, improving MAE from 5.7 to 1.2 kcal/mol; ligand ranking is target-dependent.
AI.motivation: Atomistic alchemical free-energy calculations (e.g., FEP+, OpenFE) achieve close-to-experimental accuracy but are too costly for large ligand sets. Coarse-grained models like Martini 3 are far cheaper and retain statistical-mechanical rigor, yet their accuracy for protein-ligand binding has never been assessed systematically. This work benchmarks Martini 3 against atomistic references.
AI.method: Absolute binding free energies were computed for 172 ligands across 15 protein targets using a Martini 3 double-decoupling protocol, then compared with atomistic FEP+ and OpenFE references. The systematic offset was analyzed and modeled as a linear function of the number of charged pocket residues, validated by leave-one-out cross-validation. Intra-target ligand ranking was assessed via Spearman correlation and rationalized through each series' structure-activity relationship.
AI.result: Martini underbinds for every target by 2.7–8.7 kcal/mol. The offset is systematic, comprising a uniform contribution that grows with the number of charged pocket residues. A linear model in that number (requiring only the protein structure) reduces MAE from 5.7 to 1.2 kcal/mol in leave-one-out cross-validation, close to the 1.0 kcal/mol from exact per-target offsets. title: Cooperative STT and SOT switching in perpendicular magnetic tunnel junctions: Role of the pulse-end magnetization state
summary: Spin--orbit torque MRAM (SOT-MRAM) is a leading candidate for next-generation nonvolatile memory, offering high speed, endurance, and architectural compatibility. However, in conventional SOT switching, the magnetization remains near the in-plane region at pulse termination, making the final state highly sensitive to post-pulse relaxation dynamics and prone to back-switching. To overcome this, we propose a field-free scheme in which the transverse SOT drives large-angle precessional excitation while the perpendicular spin-transfer torque (STT) biases the trajectory toward the reversed $-z$ state. Micromagnetic simulations reveal a nonlinear switching boundary in the $J_{\mathrm{STT}}$--$J_{\mathrm{SOT}}$ parameter space, originating from the distinct dynamical roles of the two torques: SOT primarily governs the excitation and crossing of the dynamical separatrix, whereas STT controls the terminal trajectory and final-state selection. An analytical macrospin model, based on the stability analysis of the current-induced equilibrium, reproduces the critical-boundary trends as functions of current density, Gilbert damping $α$, and uniaxial anisotropy $K_\mathrm{u}$, and distinguishes dynamic anti-damping and static instability branches. Systematic analyses of pulse duration, damping, anisotropy, and the STT--SOT balance further demonstrate that reliable ultrafast switching requires not only sufficient excitation to cross the separatrix before pulse termination, but also precise control of the pulse-end magnetization state to minimize post-pulse relaxation. These results establish that the pulse-end state, rather than the instantaneous torque amplitude, is the decisive factor governing switching speed and reliability in coupled STT--SOT systems.

AI.motivation: Conventional SOT switching leaves magnetization near the in-plane region at pulse termination, so the final state is highly sensitive to post-pulse relaxation and prone to back-switching. A field-free, reliable, ultrafast switching mechanism is needed.
AI.method: Field-free scheme where transverse SOT provides large-angle precessional excitation and perpendicular STT biases the trajectory toward the reversed -z state. title: Electric and Heat Transport in One-Dimensional SNS Junctions with Energy-Dependent Transmission
summary: We investigate the phase-independent dc components of the electric and heat currents through a one-dimensional superconductor-normal-metal-superconductor (SNS) junction subject to chemical-potential and temperature differences between two superconducting reservoirs. Using a scattering approach based on the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, we incorporate multiple Andreev reflections while retaining the energy dependence of transmission through the normal region. We compare energy-independent, quantum-dot-type, and quantum-point-contact transmission profiles. At low bias, both currents exhibit nonlinear features associated with the superconducting gap and multiple Andreev reflections. Their responses to a temperature difference depend remarkably on the transmission profile. At a small finite bias, the electric current depends weakly on the temperature difference for the energy-independent and quantum-dot-type profiles, whereas the quantum-point-contact profile produces a pronounced nonlinear response. The heat current depends nonlinearly on the temperature difference for all three profiles over the parameter range investigated. These results highlight the role of the transmission profile in nonlinear electric and heat transport through SNS junctions and provide a microscopic reference for related transport studies in mesoscopic fermionic superfluid junctions.

AI.motivation: Transport through SNS junctions usually assumes simplified or energy-independent transmission, leaving unclear how the detailed transmission profile shapes the interplay of superconducting-gap nonlinearities, multiple Andreev reflections, and combined voltage and temperature biases in electric and heat currents.
AI.method: A scattering approach based on the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations is used to compute phase-independent dc electric and heat currents through a one-dimensional SNS junction subject to chemical-potential and temperature differences. Multiple Andreev reflections are included while retaining the energy dependence of transmission through the normal region. Three transmission profiles are compared: energy-independent, quantum-dot-type, and quantum-point-contact.

Temperature-difference responses depend markedly on the transmission profile. At small finite bias, the electric current depends weakly on the temperature difference for energy-independent and quantum-dot-type profiles, but the quantum-point-contact profile yields a pronounced nonlinear response. The heat current depends nonlinearly on the temperature difference for all three profiles across the studied parameter range.
