title: Achieving room temperature plasticity in TiO2 ceramics by flash processing
summary: Ceramics are indispensable materials for modern engineering and high-technology applications. However, the intrinsic brittleness at room temperature can cause catastrophic failure and severely limit their widespread applications. Here, we report a flash processing (FP) method based on the coupling of electric and thermal fields to significantly improve the room-temperature plasticity of TiO2 ceramics with a large plastic compressive strain of 15.4% during micropillar compression. This large room-temperature plasticity is attributed to the proliferation of stacking faults and twin boundaries during the loading process, which may be assisted by the high concentration of oxygen vacancies introduced by the FP method. Our findings suggest that FP can be a simple and effective method for achieving improved room-temperature plasticity of ceramic materials through defect engineering.

AI.tldr: A flash processing (FP) method coupling electric and thermal fields is reported to improve the room-temperature plasticity of TiO2 ceramics, achieving 15.4% plastic compressive strain during micropillar compression.
AI.motivation: Ceramics are indispensable for modern engineering and high-technology applications, but their intrinsic brittleness at room temperature causes catastrophic failure and severely limits widespread applications. There is therefore a need for an effective method to improve the room-temperature plasticity of ceramics.
AI.method: The authors apply a flash processing (FP) method based on the coupling of electric and thermal fields to TiO2 ceramics, and evaluate the resulting room-temperature plasticity through micropillar compression testing. Microstructural analysis is used to identify the deformation mechanisms.
AI.result: The FP-treated TiO2 ceramics exhibit a large plastic compressive strain of 15.4% during micropillar compression at room temperature. This large plasticity is attributed to the proliferation of stacking faults and twin boundaries during loading, potentially assisted by the high concentration of oxygen vacancies introduced by the FP method.
AI.conclusion: Flash processing can serve as a simple and effective method for achieving improved room-temperature plasticity of ceramic materials through defect engineering.

title: Probing $L_z$ Orbital Angular Momentum via Wavefunction-Interference-Induced Charge Order
summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) characterization is central to understanding quantum materials such as valley Hall and Rashba systems and, through its connection to Berry curvature, provides key insight into band topology. Conventional OAM detection via photoemission dichroism, however, is susceptible to interference artifacts and is largely restricted to occupied states. Here, we demonstrate a real-space approach to map the $L_z$ OAM character using scanning tunneling microscopy in triangular atomic monolayers. Unlike photoemission, this method exploits interference effects arising from the $L_z$ orbital phase and the Bloch phase associated with neighboring atoms. This shifts the local density of states (LDOS) maxima to distinct Wyckoff positions between atoms, encoding $L_z$ information into characteristic real-space LDOS patterns. We exemplify this approach in 2D quantum materials with contrasting $L_z$ sequences, namely Tl/Si(111) and In/SiC(0001) monolayers, identifying $L_z$-dependent LDOS accumulation associated with distinct topological phases in both systems. Our results establish $L_z$-dependent charge localization as a proxy to atomic obstruction for energetically isolated states in triangular lattices, including transition-metal dichalcogenides.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a real-space STM-based method to map the $L_z$ orbital angular momentum character in triangular atomic monolayers by exploiting interference between the orbital phase and the Bloch phase, encoding $L_z$ into characteristic LDOS patterns at distinct Wyckoff positions.
AI.motivation: Conventional OAM detection via photoemission dichroism suffers from interference artifacts and is largely restricted to occupied states, limiting its reliability and applicability for probing band topology and quantum materials.
AI.method: The authors use scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) on triangular atomic monolayers, exploiting interference between the $L_z$ orbital phase and the Bloch phase of neighboring atoms. This shifts LDOS maxima to distinct Wyckoff positions between atoms, encoding $L_z$ information into real-space LDOS patterns. They demonstrate the approach on Tl/Si(111) and In/SiC(0001) monolayers with contrasting $L_z$ sequences.
AI.result: $L_z$-dependent LDOS accumulation is identified and linked to distinct topological phases in both Tl/Si(111) and In/SiC(0001) systems.
AI.conclusion: $L_z$-dependent charge localization serves as a proxy for atomic obstruction for energetically isolated states in triangular lattices, including transition-metal dichalcogenides, establishing a real-space OAM characterization method.

title: The role of density in shaping electron trapping in amorphous silicon nitride
summary: The electronic properties of amorphous silicon nitride vary with processing, which often changes stoichiometry and density together. Separating their contributions is essential to connect film structure with electron trapping. Across 499 stoichiometric configurations spanning 2.86-3.19g cm$^{-3}$, porosity controls the trapping mixture. Lower density increases accessible void fraction from 8.4 to 12.6%, expands internal surface and more than triples the supply of free three-coordinate Si precursors. Capture at pre-existing Si dangling bonds (K centres) rises from 9 to 29%, while induced-K and polaronic trapping decline. A neutral precursor fingerprint predicts the trapping mixture in held-out configurations and reproduces its density dependence. Local compensation controls K-centre activation, electronic competition selects capture, and bond strain predicts polaronic relaxation or induced-K formation. Routes involve distinct network volumes but retain their characteristic depths and relaxation energies across the density range. At fixed stoichiometry, density controls the trapping mixture through porosity and precursor availability.

AI.tldr: Across 499 stoichiometric amorphous silicon nitride configurations (2.86–3.19 g/cm³), density—via porosity—governs the electron-trapping mixture: lower density raises void fraction, internal surface, and free three-coordinate Si precursor supply, shifting capture toward pre-existing K centres (9→29%) while suppressing induced-K and polaronic trapping.
AI.motivation: Processing alters both stoichiometry and density of amorphous silicon nitride, making their individual effects on electronic properties hard to disentangle. Separating the density contribution is essential to link film structure to electron trapping.
AI.method: Generates and analyzes 499 stoichiometric configurations covering a density range of 2.86–3.19 g/cm³. Quantifies void fraction, internal surface area, and free three-coordinate Si precursor supply. Classifies trapping pathways (pre-existing Si dangling bonds / K centres, induced-K, polaronic), identifies a neutral precursor fingerprint, and tests its predictive power on held-out configurations. Correlates local compensation with K-centre activation, electronic competition with capture selection, and bond strain with polaronic relaxation versus induced-K formation.
AI.result: Lower density increases accessible void fraction from 8.4% to 12.6%, expands internal surface, and more than triples free three-coordinate Si precursor supply. Capture at pre-existing K centres rises from 9% to 29%, while induced-K and polaronic trapping decline. AI.conclusion: At fixed stoichiometry, density controls the electron-trapping mixture through porosity and precursor availability. Local compensation governs K-centre activation, electronic competition selects the capture channel, and bond strain dictates polaronic relaxation versus induced-K formation.

title: Epitaxial growth of WO3 on r-plane sapphire by hot-filament metal-oxide deposition using CO2 as a precursor
summary: The deposition of epitaxial films of WO3 by hot-filament metal-oxide deposition using CO2 as a precursor was demonstrated. The films were obtained at a low growth rate of 0.25 nm/min. The optical properties of the film were assessed by variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry, indicating transparency across the visible spectrum and high absorption above 3 eV.

AI.tldr: Epitaxial WO3 films were grown by hot-filament metal-oxide deposition using CO2 as a precursor at a low rate of 0.25 nm/min; ellipsometry shows visible transparency and strong absorption above 3 eV.
AI.motivation: The paper explores a CO2-based precursor route for depositing epitaxial WO3 thin films, a material of interest for optical and optoelectronic applications, addressing the need for controlled epitaxial growth.
AI.method: Hot-filament metal-oxide deposition with CO2 as the oxygen precursor was used to grow epitaxial WO3 films. Optical properties were characterized by variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry.
AI.result: Epitaxial WO3 films were successfully deposited at a low growth rate of 0.25 nm/min. Ellipsometry revealed transparency in the visible spectrum and high absorption above 3 eV.
AI.conclusion: CO2 is a viable precursor for hot-filament deposition of epitaxial WO3 films, which exhibit promising optical characteristics—visible transparency and strong UV absorption above 3 eV.

title: Predicting plasmonic pole representations of complex dielectric spectra using convolutional neural networks
summary: Extracting spectral properties such as energy position, broadening, and spectral weight from dielectric spectra is critical for interpreting collective electronic excitations in many-body physics. Conventional approaches typically rely on nonlinear fitting procedures that can be computationally demanding and highly sensitive to initialization and fitting choices. In this work, we develop a convolutional neural-network framework for the direct inversion of dielectric spectra into their underlying plasmonic pole structures using a multipole-Padé representation. Rather than training on a constrained database of spectra associated with a specific set of materials, the network is trained entirely on synthetic spectra generated from the analytical multipole-Padé expression with randomized parameters. This enables the network to learn the general mapping between the spectra and their features in an unbiased way, without requiring large, material-specific datasets derived from real materials. We demonstrate that the synthetically trained network generalizes to complex first-principles and experimental dielectric spectra, extracting the underlying pole parameters with high accuracy in a single forward pass. This approach provides an efficient and robust alternative to conventional nonlinear fitting, enabling high-throughput, automated analysis of dielectric spectra across diverse materials and applications.

AI.tldr: A CNN trained entirely on synthetic multipole-Padé spectra directly inverts dielectric spectra into plasmonic pole parameters in a single forward pass, generalizing to first-principles and experimental data.
AI.motivation: Extracting spectral properties (energy position, broadening, spectral weight) from dielectric spectra is essential for interpreting collective electronic excitations in many-body physics, but conventional nonlinear fitting is computationally demanding and sensitive to initialization and fitting choices.
AI.method: A convolutional neural-network framework is developed for direct inversion of dielectric spectra into underlying plasmonic pole structures, using a multipole-Padé representation. The network is trained entirely on synthetic spectra generated from the analytical multipole-Padé expression with randomized parameters, rather than a constrained, material-specific database, enabling unbiased learning of the general spectrum-to-feature mapping.
AI.result: The synthetically trained network generalizes to complex first-principles and experimental dielectric spectra, extracting underlying pole parameters with high accuracy in a single forward pass.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers an efficient and robust alternative to conventional nonlinear fitting, enabling high-throughput, automated analysis of dielectric spectra across diverse materials and applications.

title: Interlayer ferromagnetic order revealed through pressure-enhanced interlayer exchange coupling in Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$
summary: Van der Waals ferromagnets possess finite interlayer magnetic coupling despite their layered crystal structures, and this coupling plays an important role in determining their magnetic properties. In this study, we performed magnetization measurements on high-quality Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ single crystals while selectively tuning the interlayer coupling using hydrostatic pressure. We identified two characteristic temperatures, $T_{\rm inf1}$ and $T_{\rm inf2}$, below the Curie temperature with opposite pressure dependences: $T_{\rm inf1}$ is associated with thermally activated domain-wall depinning, whereas $T_{\rm inf2}$ reflects the formation of interlayer ferromagnetic order. Both temperatures exhibit pronounced pressure dependences, in sharp contrast to the nearly pressure-independent Curie temperature associated with intralayer ferromagnetic order. First-principles calculations revealed a substantial pressure-induced enhancement of the interlayer exchange interaction and reasonably reproduced $T_{\rm inf2}$ and its pressure dependence. These results demonstrate that the emergence of interlayer magnetic ordering can be predicted from the microscopic interlayer exchange coupling, establishing a predictive framework for understanding and designing interlayer coupling phenomena in layered magnetic materials.

AI.tldr: By applying hydrostatic pressure to Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ single crystals, the authors identify two sub-Curie characteristic temperatures with opposite pressure dependences and show that the formation of interlayer ferromagnetic order is governed by the pressure-tunable microscopic interlayer exchange coupling.
AI.motivation: Van der Waals ferromagnets exhibit finite interlayer magnetic coupling despite their layered structures, and this coupling strongly affects their magnetic properties. However, a predictive microscopic understanding of how interlayer coupling governs interlayer magnetic ordering remains lacking.
AI.method: Magnetization measurements were performed on high-quality Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ single crystals under tunable hydrostatic pressure to selectively modify interlayer coupling. First-principles calculations were used to evaluate the pressure dependence of the interlayer exchange interaction.
AI.result: Two characteristic temperatures below the Curie temperature, $T_{\rm inf1}$ and $T_{\rm inf2}$, were identified with opposite pressure dependences: $T_{\rm inf1}$ corresponds to thermally activated domain-wall depinning, while $T_{\rm inf2}$ reflects interlayer ferromagnetic order formation. AI.conclusion: The emergence of interlayer magnetic ordering can be predicted from the microscopic interlayer exchange coupling, providing a predictive framework for understanding and designing interlayer coupling phenomena in layered magnetic materials.

title: A General Algorithm for Minimal Uncoupled Stress--Strain Calculations of Elastic Constant
summary: We have developed a general algorithm for constructing the minimum number of strain configurations required to extract second-order elastic constants from first-principles stress-strain calculations without algebraic coupling between the constants targeted for extraction. The method operates on the sparsity structure of the symmetry-reduced elastic stiffness matrix, represented by an auxiliary binary matrix, and generates admissible strain patterns algorithmically rather than prescribing separate strain sets for individual crystal symmetries. Each independent elastic constant is obtained from a single stress component, while additional stress relations generated by the same deformation provide internal consistency checks. Because the six-dimensional strain space contains only 2^6-1=63 non-empty strain patterns, the minimality of the resulting sets can be verified exactly for every elastic-symmetry type considered. The construction reproduces established high-efficiency strain sets in cases where they are minimal and yields improved sets for symmetry classes in which previously tabulated schemes require additional configurations. Because the formulation is based on stress-strain derivatives, it can also be readily extended to finite temperatures using consistently sampled ensemble-averaged thermodynamic stresses. Explicit strain sets are derived for all elastic-symmetry types spanning the 230 crystallographic space groups, and their accuracy and computational efficiency are benchmarked against established approaches.

AI.tldr: A general algorithm constructs minimal strain sets for extracting second-order elastic constants from first-principles stress-strain calculations, eliminating algebraic coupling and yielding improved sets across all elastic-symmetry types.
AI.motivation: Existing tabulated strain schemes for determining second-order elastic constants often require more configurations than necessary, and separate strain sets are usually prescribed for each crystal symmetry, lacking a unified, provably minimal construction.
AI.method: The method operates on the sparsity structure of the symmetry-reduced elastic stiffness matrix via an auxiliary binary matrix, algorithmically generating admissible strain patterns rather than prescribing them per symmetry. Each independent elastic constant is extracted from a single stress component, with additional stress relations from the same deformation serving as internal consistency checks. Minimality is verified by exhaustive enumeration of the 63 non-empty strain patterns in the six-dimensional strain space.

title: Photoinduced Odd- and Mixed-Parity Magnetism in Collinear Antiferromagnets
summary: Altermagnetism, characterized by compensated collinear magnetic moments in real space and momentum-dependent spin splitting with even-parity symmetry, has recently emerged as a distinct form of magnetic order beyond the conventional ferro- and antiferromagnetic paradigms. However, realizing odd- and mixed-parity magnetism in fully compensated collinear magnets remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that light irradiation can induce odd- and mixed-parity magnetism in conventional collinear antiferromagnets. Taking monolayer CoS and CoSe as representative systems, and combining Floquet theory with first-principles calculations, we show that circularly polarized light (CPL) induces odd-parity $f$-wave spin splitting, whereas elliptically polarized light (EPL) induces odd-parity $p$-wave spin splitting. Uniaxial strain combined with CPL provides an alternative route to realizing the $p$-wave state. More remarkably, applying an electric field together with CPL or EPL transforms the spin splitting into mixed-parity forms. The light-induced breaking of $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry, together with spin-orbit coupling, further gives rise to a finite anomalous Hall response. Our work establishes a versatile strategy for engineering odd- and mixed-parity spin splitting in compensated antiferromagnets, offering a route toward light-controlled electronic and magnetic phenomena.

AI.tldr: Light irradiation (circular or elliptical polarization, optionally with strain or electric field) induces odd- and mixed-parity spin splitting in conventional collinear antiferromagnets like monolayer CoS and CoSe, enabling a finite anomalous Hall response.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetism features compensated collinear moments with even-parity momentum-dependent spin splitting, but realizing odd- and mixed-parity magnetism in fully compensated collinear magnets remains challenging.
AI.method: Uses Floquet theory combined with first-principles calculations on monolayer CoS and CoSe, applying circularly polarized light (CPL), elliptically polarized light (EPL), uniaxial strain, and electric fields.
AI.result: CPL induces odd-parity f-wave spin splitting; EPL induces odd-parity p-wave spin splitting. Uniaxial strain plus CPL offers an alternative route to the p-wave state. Electric field with CPL or EPL yields mixed-parity spin splitting. Light-induced breaking of PT symmetry with spin-orbit coupling produces a finite anomalous Hall response.
AI.conclusion: Provides a versatile strategy for engineering odd- and mixed-parity spin splitting in compensated antiferromagnets, offering a route toward light-controlled electronic and magnetic phenomena.

title: Solution-Based Synthesis of Fe-Co-Ni Prussian Blue Analogue Powders: A Comparative Structural, Spectroscopic and Thermal Study
summary: Prussian Blue (Fe-PBA) and its Co and Ni analogues (Co-PBA and Ni-PBA) were synthesized by an additive-free aqueous co-precipitation route using K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] and FeCl$_3$, CoCl$_2$, or NiCl$_2$, respectively. The three powders were systematically compared by X-ray diffraction, ATR-FTIR and Raman spectroscopy, FEG-SEM/EDS, and TG/SDTA. All compositions exhibit the characteristic cubic cyanide-bridged PBA framework, with apparent lattice parameters of 10.10 +/- 0.02, 10.01 +/- 0.02, and 10.10 +/- 0.03 Angstrom for Fe-PBA, Co-PBA, and Ni-PBA, respectively. The dominant C$\equiv$N stretching band in ATR-FTIR shifts from 2062 to 2071 and 2087 cm$^{-1}$ across the Fe-Co-Ni series, indicating composition-dependent changes in the local cyanide environment. Fe-PBA contains less potassium than the Co- and Ni-containing powders and exhibits a substantially larger low-temperature mass loss. Sharp reflections assigned to crystalline KCl are observed in all three diffraction patterns, while additional unassigned reflections in Ni-PBA indicate the presence of at least one further crystalline phase. These results show that differences among Fe-, Co-, and Ni-based PBAs cannot be attributed solely to transition-metal identity, as precursor oxidation state and washing efficiency also influence the composition and thermal response of the resulting powders.

title: Benchmarking Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Temperature-Dependent Elasticity of Binary and High-Entropy Refractory Carbides
summary: Accurate prediction of temperature-dependent elasticity is important for assessing refractory carbides under high-temperature conditions, but the computational cost of ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) limits systematic investigations across compositions and temperatures. Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) offer an efficient alternative, yet their accuracy for this task remains insufficiently established. Here, we benchmark nine uMLIPs against consistent AIMD reference data for five binary and two high-entropy (HE) carbides between 300 and 1200 K. Elastic constants and the corresponding bulk, shear, and Young's moduli are obtained using stress-strain molecular dynamics, explicitly sampling thermal atomic motion and anharmonic effects beyond thermal expansion alone. We assess absolute elastic properties and normalized thermal softening separately. MACE-MH-1 achieves the lowest overall mean absolute percentage error (5.7%). MACE-MH-1 and DPA4-Mini reproduce thermal softening most accurately, with mean deviations of 2.5 and 2.3 percentage points, respectively. All models generally underestimate stiffness, with larger equilibrium volumes relative to the AIMD reference likely contributing to this trend for most models. C12 exhibits the largest model-dependent errors. The HE carbides are described with accuracy comparable to that of the binary carbides, indicating no apparent accuracy penalty from chemical complexity. Accuracy instead varies with transition-metal composition, with group-V carbides, particularly TaC, presenting the greatest challenge. These results identify promising pretrained models for finite-temperature elasticity in carbides and show why accurate absolute stiffness and thermal softening must be assessed independently.

AI.tldr: Nine universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are benchmarked against AIMD for temperature-dependent elasticity of five binary and two high-entropy carbides (300–1200 K). MACE-MH-1 gives the lowest overall error (5.7% MAPE), while MACE-MH-1 and DPA4-Mini best reproduce thermal softening; all models tend to underestimate stiffness, with group-V (especially TaC) carbides hardest to describe.
AI.motivation: Assessing refractory carbides under high-temperature conditions requires accurate temperature-dependent elasticity, but the computational cost of AIMD prevents systematic studies across compositions and temperatures. uMLIPs are a promising efficient alternative, yet their accuracy for this task has not been sufficiently established.
AI.method: Benchmark nine uMLIPs against consistent AIMD reference data for five binary and two high-entropy carbides between 300 and 1200 K. Elastic constants and bulk, shear, and Young's moduli are computed via stress-strain molecular dynamics, explicitly sampling thermal atomic motion and anharmonic effects beyond thermal expansion alone. MACE-MH-1 and DPA4-Mini reproduce thermal softening most accurately (mean deviations of 2.5 and 2.3 percentage points). All models generally underestimate stiffness, likely linked to larger equilibrium volumes relative to AIMD for most models. C12 shows the largest model-dependent errors. High-entropy carbides are described with accuracy comparable to binary carbides, with no apparent penalty from chemical complexity; accuracy instead varies with transition-metal composition, group-V carbides (especially TaC) being the most challenging.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies promising pretrained uMLIP models for finite-temperature elasticity in carbides and demonstrates that accurate absolute stiffness and thermal softening must be evaluated independently, since performance on the two metrics is not equivalent.

title: Beyond special quasirandom structures: free energies from energy cumulants
summary: Predicting the finite-temperature stability of a disordered phase requires its free energy. It is traditionally approximated by combining the energy of a special quasirandom structure (a small cell mimicking a random alloy) with the ideal configurational entropy. This approximation neglects the short-range order that develops on cooling. In this study, we show that the conventional approximation is the first term of an infinite expansion of the free energy in energy cumulants. Higher-order cumulants are estimated from energies of random arrangements, without Monte Carlo or molecular dynamics. In a nine-element refractory system, adding the second cumulant reduced free energy errors by about an order of magnitude. The expansion gives phase diagrams with order--disorder transitions, defect concentrations, and short-range order. To demonstrate its utility, we used a foundation interatomic potential to screen lithium-excess rocksalt oxides across 26 elements for synthesizable disordered phases rich in the Li$_4$ clusters needed for lithium percolation. The approach applies to any lattice and chemistry, and brings disordered phases within reach of routine screening.

AI.tldr: Finite-temperature stability of disordered phases is traditionally approximated by combining special quasirandom structure energy with ideal configurational entropy, ignoring short-range order. This work recasts that approximation as the first term of an infinite cumulant expansion of the free energy, estimating higher-order cumulants from energies of random arrangements without Monte Carlo or molecular dynamics.
AI.motivation: The conventional approximation neglects short-range order that develops on cooling, limiting accuracy in predicting finite-temperature stability of disordered phases. There is a need for a method that captures short-range order while remaining computationally cheap enough for routine screening across chemistries and lattices.
AI.method: The free energy is expressed as an infinite expansion in energy cumulants, with the conventional special quasirandom structure plus ideal configurational entropy appearing as the first term. Higher-order cumulants are estimated from the energies of random arrangements, avoiding Monte Carlo or molecular dynamics. A foundation interatomic potential is used to screen lithium-excess rocksalt oxides across 26 elements for synthesizable disordered phases rich in Li4 clusters needed for lithium percolation.
AI.result: In a nine-element refractory system, adding the second cumulant reduced free energy errors by about an order of magnitude. The expansion yields phase diagrams with order-disorder transitions, defect concentrations, and short-range order, and was applied to screen Li-excess rocksalt oxides across 26 elements.
AI.conclusion: The cumulant expansion generalizes the standard disordered-phase free energy approximation, captures short-range order at low cost, applies to any lattice and chemistry, and brings disordered phases within reach of routine screening.

title: Comprehensive study of massively overlapping cascades in common elemental metals
summary: Massively overlapping cascades simulations were carried out in 21 elemental metals: Be, Al, Ti, V, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zr, Nb, Mo, Rh, Pd, Ag, Hf, Ta, W, Pt, Au and Pb. These elements have simple FCC, BCC and HCP lattice structures. For each element, 2000 cumulative 5 keV cascades were simulated using molecular dynamics. The overlapping cascades were simulated using various classical analytical interatomic potentials as well as with machine-learning interatomic potentials for many of the elements. The general conclusion is that results from massively overlapping cascades simulations are very sensitive to the choice of interatomic potential across the periodic table. Furthermore, we see that FCC metals all form stacking fault tetrahedra due to irradiation, and also typically include interstitial type Shockley partial and Frank type dislocations. In BCC materials typically form interstitial 1/2$\langle$1 1 1$\rangle$ dislocations, but vacancy type 1/2$\langle$1 1 1$\rangle$ dislocations were also observed in V and Nb. HCP materials tend to form complex dislocation structures mainly consisting of a-type dislocations that can be of both vacancy or interstitial type. Correlations between saturated defect concentrations and fundamental underlying material properties are explored.

AI.tldr: Massively overlapping 5 keV cascade simulations in 21 elemental metals reveal strong sensitivity of defect results to the interatomic potential, with distinct dislocation and defect structures forming in FCC, BCC, and HCP lattices.
AI.motivation: Radiation damage accumulation under prolonged irradiation involves overlapping cascades, so understanding how cumulative damage evolves is essential for predicting material performance; the study also aims to assess how results depend on the chosen interatomic potential.
AI.method: Molecular dynamics was used to simulate 2000 cumulative 5 keV cascades per element for 21 metals (Be, Al, Ti, V, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zr, Nb, Mo, Rh, Pd, Ag, Hf, Ta, W, Pt, Au, Pb) with FCC, BCC and HCP structures, employing classical analytical and machine-learning interatomic potentials.
AI.result: Massively overlapping cascade results are very sensitive to the interatomic potential. FCC metals form stacking fault tetrahedra with interstitial-type Shockley partial and Frank dislocations; BCC metals typically form interstitial 1/2<111> dislocations, with vacancy-type 1/2<111> dislocations also seen in V and Nb; HCP metals form complex a-type dislocation structures of vacancy and/or interstitial type. Correlations between saturated defect concentrations and fundamental material properties were explored.
AI.conclusion: The choice of interatomic potential strongly governs overlapping-cascade simulation outcomes across the periodic table, and defect/dislocation structures exhibit clear crystal-structure-dependent trends. Saturated defect concentrations correlate with underlying material properties.

title: Multifunctional synaptic learning and neuromorphic computing using crystalline TiO$_x$/NiO$_x$ heterojunction-based memory devices
summary: An attempt is made here to mimic different properties of biological synapses using Ag/TiO$_x$/NiO$_x$/p$^{++}$-Si memristor structure by studying its different transport properties under dc and pulsed bias. The presence of crystalline NiO$_x$ with smaller gains is found to be helpful to get TiO$_x$ deposited on its top with crystalline properties and larger grains. The heterostructure offers stable bipolar forming free non-volatile resistive switching characteristics under reverse biased condition with gradual set and reset features. These devices are also able to successfully implement the classical Pavlov's learning, study artificial nociceptor and Morse code detection. While incorporating synaptic weights derived from the measured conductance programming pulse relationship, an artificial neural network achieves nearly 95\% accuracy in MNIST digit recognition. In brief, NiO$_x$/TiO$_x$ heterojunction plays the pivotal role in getting such reproducible $I-V$ characteristics for mimicking different properties of biological synapses.

AI.tldr: A Ag/TiO$_x$/NiO$_x$/p$^{++}$-Si memristor is shown to emulate biological synaptic functions, including Pavlovian learning, nociception, and Morse code detection, while supporting ~95% MNIST digit recognition accuracy.
AI.motivation: Biological synapses exhibit diverse adaptive behaviors, and hardware that mimics them is sought for neuromorphic computing; a suitable memristive heterostructure with stable, forming-free analog switching is needed.
AI.method: Characterize transport properties of the Ag/TiO$_x$/NiO$_x$/p$^{++}$-Si structure under dc and pulsed bias, exploiting crystalline NiO$_x$ as a template for crystalline, large-grain TiO$_x$ in a heterojunction; measure conductance-programming-pulse relationship and implement synaptic plasticity functions.
AI.result: The heterostructure shows stable bipolar forming-free non-volatile resistive switching under reverse bias with gradual set/reset features; implements Pavlov's learning, artificial nociceptor behavior, and Morse code detection; and an artificial neural network using its synaptic weights reaches nearly 95% accuracy in MNIST recognition.
AI.conclusion: The NiO$_x$/TiO$_x$ heterojunction is pivotal in achieving reproducible I-V characteristics for mimicking diverse biological synaptic properties, demonstrating potential for neuromorphic hardware.

title: Emergent gold-induced interfacial magnetism in monolayer FePS$_3$
summary: Owing to their atomically clean interfaces and extreme thinness, two-dimensional (2D) materials are ideal hosts for strong proximity effects, whereby contact with an adjacent material reshapes their ground state. Here, we demonstrate such an effect within a hybrid heterostructure, between the 2D antiferromagnet FePS$_3$ and an ultrathin gold film. Rather than a passive support, the latter profoundly changes the nature of the magnetism in the 2D magnet, inducing a sizeable interfacial moment. Large-area flakes from Au-assisted exfoliation, combined with element-selective X-ray absorption mapping, enable a layer-by-layer study from monolayer to bulk, benchmarked against an inert SiO$_2$ substrate reference. At 9 T and 5 K, the monolayer on gold shows a three-fold enhanced X-ray magnetic circular dichroism relative to SiO$_2$, with a $\sim$40% reduction of the orbital-to-spin moment ratio. Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering reveals a collapse of the crystal-field (d-d) excitations and a massive spectral-weight transfer to the charge-transfer region, unveiling the microscopic mechanism behind this change. Supported by atomic multiplet calculations, we identify interfacial charge transfer and Fe 3d-Au hybridization as the origin of these effects, which decay over the first three layers and vanish at the pentalayer, establishing layer number combined with substrate engineering as an atomically precise handle.

AI.tldr: A FePS₃/Au heterostructure reveals a strong proximity effect where ultrathin gold induces an interfacial magnetic moment, driven by interfacial charge transfer and Fe 3d–Au hybridization, decaying over three layers.
AI.motivation: Two-dimensional materials are ideal platforms for strong proximity effects because of their atomically clean interfaces and extreme thinness, where an adjacent material can reshape the ground state. The authors aim to demonstrate such an effect in a hybrid heterostructure by showing that gold is not merely a passive support but profoundly alters the magnetic ground state of the 2D antiferromagnet FePS₃.
AI.method: Large-area flakes obtained by Au-assisted exfoliation combined with element-selective X-ray absorption mapping enabled layer-by-layer study from monolayer to bulk, benchmarked against an inert SiO₂ substrate. X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) quantified the moment change and orbital-to-spin ratio; resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) probed crystal-field (d-d) excitations and charge-transfer spectral weight. Atomic multiplet calculations supported the interpretation.
AI.result: At 9 T and 5 K, the FePS₃ monolayer on gold shows a three-fold enhanced XMCD relative to SiO₂, with a ~40% reduction of the orbital-to-spin moment ratio. RIXS reveals a collapse of crystal-field (d-d) excitations and a massive spectral-weight transfer to the charge-transfer region. The effects decay over the first three layers and vanish at the pentalayer.
AI.conclusion: The interfacial charge transfer and Fe 3d–Au hybridization are identified as the microscopic origin of the modified magnetism. Layer number combined with substrate engineering provides an atomically precise handle to tune the magnetic ground state of 2D magnets.

title: Direct Quantification of Molecular Helicity-Dependent Effective Magnetic Fields in Chiral Polypeptide/Ferromagnet Heterostructures
summary: Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) refers to structural chirality governing spin transport in chiral systems, with experimental signatures reported in both transport experiments and photoemission. Beyond influencing transport, recent experiments indicate that adsorbed chiral molecules can influence the magnetic state of adjacent ferromagnetic layers, suggesting the existence of chirality-induced effects whose origin and quantitative characterization remain lacking. Here, we investigate chirality-induced long-range magnetic interactions in a hybrid molecular/ferromagnetic multilayer beyond the conventional direct transport coupling. We demonstrate the long-range nature by decoupling the adsorbed chiral molecules from the magnet using an insulating spacer. We show that self-assembled monolayers of chiral polypeptides with a helical structure can act on a ferromagnetic multilayer via an enantiomer-dependent effective magnetic field that may be mediated by chiral phonons through the insulating layer. Using Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect (MOKE) microscopy with on-chip reference regions free of molecules, we directly quantify this field by measuring precisely the reproducible shifts of the local hysteresis loops. The extracted effective field reverses sign for opposite enantiomers and correlates with the enantiomeric excess. These results provide a direct and quantitative link between molecular chirality and magnetic response in hybrid heterostructures, establishing an experimentally accessible benchmark for a CISS-related effect.

AI.tldr: Adsorbed chiral polypeptide monolayers exert an enantiomer-dependent effective magnetic field on a ferromagnetic multilayer through an insulating spacer, quantified via MOKE microscopy.
AI.motivation: Chirality-induced spin selectivity is well documented in transport and photoemission, and recent experiments suggest adsorbed chiral molecules can modify the magnetic state of adjacent ferromagnets. However, the origin and quantitative characterization of these chirality-induced magnetic effects remain lacking.
AI.method: The authors study a hybrid molecular/ferromagnetic multilayer and decouple the adsorbed chiral molecules from the magnet using an insulating spacer to test the long-range nature of the interaction. Self-assembled monolayers of helical chiral polypeptides are used, and Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect (MOKE) microscopy with on-chip molecule-free reference regions is employed to directly measure reproducible shifts of local hysteresis loops.
AI.result: An enantiomer-dependent effective magnetic field acts on the ferromagnetic multilayer, possibly mediated by chiral phonons through the insulating layer. The extracted effective field reverses sign for opposite enantiomers and correlates with the enantiomeric excess.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a direct, quantitative link between molecular chirality and magnetic response in hybrid heterostructures, establishing an experimentally accessible benchmark for a CISS-related effect.

title: Specialized machine learning force fields for materials dynamics
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming atomistic simulations by accessing unprecedented length and time scales. While pretrained equivariant graph neural networks achieve robust zero-shot performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, their translation to complex materials dynamics remains fundamentally challenged by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling limits. In this Review, we examine how physics-driven specialization extends the applicability of MLIPs to complex dynamical systems. We systematically evaluate the structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. Through four demanding application contexts - electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture - we establish a framework for observable-specific validation. Highlighting the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, we emphasize that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables. We conclude with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

AI.tldr: This review argues that physics-driven specialization is needed to extend machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) from near-equilibrium, zero-shot tasks to complex materials dynamics, and proposes observable-specific validation across four demanding applications.
AI.motivation: Pretrained equivariant graph neural networks deliver robust zero-shot MLIP performance for near-equilibrium properties across broad chemical spaces, but their extension to complex materials dynamics is fundamentally limited by out-of-distribution reactive states, representation biases, and computational scaling constraints.
AI.method: A systematic review and evaluation of structural trade-offs in MLIP design: the undersampling of highly strained configurations, the prohibitive computational overhead of high-order message-passing architectures, and the necessity of nonlocal interactions for open and field-coupled systems. The framework is developed and tested through four demanding application contexts: electrified interfaces, compositionally fluctuating open systems, multiphase evolution, and large-scale fracture.
AI.result: The review establishes a framework for observable-specific validation of MLIPs, and highlights the complementary roles of universal foundation models and task-specific potentials, emphasizing that targeted adaptations must be rigorously benchmarked against intended observables.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes with a roadmap for developing physically consistent, hardware-aware force fields that seamlessly connect electronic-structure accuracy to macroscopic materials phenomena.

title: A Universal Polybromide Melt Strategy for the Direct Conversion of Metals into Optoelectronic-Grade Bromide Perovskites
summary: Halide perovskite systems require specific metal oxidation states (M2+ or M+/M3+ pairs), limiting processing flexibility during traditional synthesis and posing stability challenges for multivalent metals like Sn, Cu, and Au. This work anchors a profound paradigm shift: a universal, single-step, organic-solvent free synthetic platform that directly converts stable elemental metal films into bromide perovskite and perovskite-related systems for a wide variety of (opto)electronic applications. The synthetic platform uses methylammonium polybromide melt (PBM) that reacts at room temperature with different elemental metals, including Pb, Sn, Au, and Cu, successfully transforming them into their respective Br-perovskite phases: MAPbBr3, MASnBr3, MA2Au2Br6, and MA2CuBr4. It is shown that the PBMs chemical activity can be tuned, and in situ X-ray diffraction captures in two cases transient intermediate phases during phase evolution. For Sn, which tends towards overoxidation to Sn4+ phase, changes in the PBMs composition coupled with a metallic Sn mediated comproportionation reaction allowed suppressing overoxidation, and formation of high quality MASnBr3 films under ambient conditions. Overall, oxidation and disproportionation potentials are found to be useful metrics for predicting M:PBM reaction outcomes. Industrially, this approach should be fully compatible with roll-to-roll infrastructure, providing a low-barrier pathway to scale next-generation optoelectronic technologies.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a single-step, organic-solvent-free platform that converts stable elemental metal films (Pb, Sn, Au, Cu) directly into bromide perovskites via reaction with a methylammonium polybromide melt (PBM) at room temperature, enabling scalable, roll-to-roll fabrication of optoelectronic materials.
AI.motivation: Halide perovskites conventionally require specific metal oxidation states (M2+ or M+/M3+ pairs), which restricts processing flexibility and creates stability problems, especially for multivalent metals such as Sn, Cu, and Au that are prone to overoxidation and disproportionation.
AI.method: A universal, single-step, organic-solvent-free synthesis using a methylammonium polybromide melt (PBM) that reacts at room temperature with elemental metal films. The PBM's chemical activity is tunable; in situ X-ray diffraction tracks transient intermediate phases during phase evolution. For Sn, PBM composition adjustment combined with a metallic Sn-mediated comproportionation reaction suppresses overoxidation to Sn4+. Oxidation and disproportionation potentials are used as predictive metrics for M:PBM reaction outcomes.
AI.result: Elemental Pb, Sn, Au, and Cu films were successfully converted into MAPbBr3, MASnBr3, MA2Au2Br6, and MA2CuBr4, respectively. In situ XRD captured transient intermediate phases in two cases, and high-quality MASnBr3 films were formed under ambient conditions by suppressing Sn overoxidation.
AI.conclusion: The platform enables direct conversion of stable elemental metal films into bromide perovskite and perovskite-related systems, is compatible with roll-to-roll infrastructure, and offers a low-barrier pathway to scale next-generation optoelectronic technologies.

title: The Stability of Rutile Oxides for Oxygen Evolution Catalysis: From Mechanistic Understanding to New Descriptors
summary: Polymer electrolyte water electrolysis is considered as a pivotal technology for green hydrogen production. Iridium dioxide (IrO2) serves as the benchmark electrocatalyst for the anodic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in these cells. However, the scarcity and cost of iridium drives efforts to find durable and cost-effective replacements or drastically reduce the iridium loading. While ruthenium dioxide (RuO2) offers comparable activity, its practical utility is impacted by its stability being inferior to IrO2. The presented computational study analyzes the metal-oxygen bond strengths in bulk IrO2 and RuO2 to provide insights into the electronic origins of their differing stabilities. Through a comparative analysis of the electronic structure of bulk rutile IrO2, RuO2, and selected MO2 systems, it is able to discriminate the covalent and ionic contributions to the metal-oxygen bond using crystal-orbital-derived electronic descriptors.

AI.tldr: A computational study compares IrO2 and RuO2 to explain the electronic origins of their differing OER stability, distinguishing covalent and ionic contributions to metal-oxygen bonding via crystal-orbital-derived descriptors.
AI.motivation: Polymer electrolyte water electrolysis is key for green hydrogen, and IrO2 is the benchmark anodic OER catalyst. Yet iridium's scarcity and cost motivate finding durable, cheaper alternatives or lowering Ir loading. RuO2 shows comparable activity but inferior stability, so understanding the electronic basis of this stability gap is important.
AI.method: A computational study analyzing metal-oxygen bond strengths in bulk IrO2 and RuO2. It comparatively analyzes the electronic structure of bulk rutile IrO2, RuO2, and selected MO2 systems, using crystal-orbital-derived electronic descriptors to discriminate covalent versus ionic contributions to the metal-oxygen bond.
AI.result: Using crystal-orbital-derived electronic descriptors, the study discriminates the covalent and ionic contributions to the metal-oxygen bond in bulk rutile IrO2, RuO2, and selected MO2 systems, providing electronic-structure insights into their differing stabilities.
AI.conclusion: The presented computational analysis offers electronic-structure insight into the differing stabilities of IrO2 and RuO2 by quantifying covalent and ionic contributions to metal-oxygen bonding, which may inform the design of durable, cost-effective OER catalysts or reduced-iridium alternatives.
